concepts.body: A reusable named definition differs from one execution of a particular version.
concepts.detail: WorkflowTemplate owns activeVersion and inputSchema; WorkflowTemplateVersion owns spec JSON; WorkflowRun stores specSnapshot, timing, status and lineage.
concepts.title: Template ≠ run

concepts.body: A node is a graph instruction; an activity is a side-effect boundary.
concepts.detail: cond/set/terminate are interpreter control flow. step, agent, mcp, eval, containerStep and shell nodes are dispatched through one table that shares input resolution, retry, onFail/onError and recording; agent, mcp, eval and containerStep become named worker steps with their own executors, and shell goes to the workflow’s shell activity. Human and signal nodes wait durably.
concepts.title: Node ≠ activity

concepts.body: An agent is a versioned persona/config; a skill is prompt text; a tool executes code.
concepts.detail: AgentSkillRef orders skills. toolKeys select capabilities, and mcpConnectionId links a tool source. The implementer supports local workspace tools; a generic agent node gets them only when it asks for a checkout of the run’s repository (workspace: true), under the agent-run grant (no opinion means the read tools).
concepts.title: Agent ≠ skill ≠ tool

concepts.body: A connection identifies a team-owned external target; a workspace materializes its execution context.
concepts.detail: Connection.type/config/token describe integration targets. Providers are git_repo, document, issue_tracker, record and api_only. Registered types have uneven handler coverage.
concepts.title: Connection ≠ workspace

concepts.body: A stored input can be reused across executions; the acting launcher can change.
concepts.detail: RunInput.requestedById is submission history. WorkflowRun.launchedById identifies this launch; temporalRunId prevents trusting a reused workflow ID across executions. An Idempotency-Key on a work request binds to that user’s first submission and replays the run it started. A ticket’s workflow id is allocated with every row of the same repository (same host, owner and name compared case-insensitively, active or not) counted as one repository, so a run in flight on any of them conflicts; when the conflicting run belongs to another row, the response says the ticket is running without naming its workflow id. A retry or agent re-run keeps the request identity and adds an execution, which the Requests view groups under it. A run an event automation starts is nobody’s launch: it carries no launchedById and uses the platform credential, never a user’s saved token. A run started by labelling an issue is the one exception, and only in attribution: the labeller’s linked GitHub account must resolve to an active platform user who is a member of the repository and passes the same launch decision as any launch, and that user is recorded as requestedById; the run still acts as the platform.
concepts.title: Request ≠ launch identity

concepts.body: Spec and run-pinned settings are captured, but not every configuration read is frozen.
concepts.detail: GLOBAL agent version maps, skill revisions and run-pinned settings are captured at run start; more-specific agent rows resolve their current active versions. A run-pinned key missing from a run’s snapshot is pinned the first time an activity’s request context reads it, at the value that read resolves, and a value already pinned is never replaced; a channel turn’s run is pinned at its own start and backfilled at its Slack channel’s scope, and a failed backfill falls back to the live value until the next lookup. Each agent’s runtime is pinned on the run at start, or at first resolution for an agent the start snapshot lacks. Non-run-pinned settings and credentials can change. This is selective reproducibility, not a hermetically frozen run. A credential pinned by an agent is not frozen either: the worker checks it on each resolution (behind the config cache) and falls back, with a warning, to the provider cascade if the pin is missing, belongs to another provider, or is out of scope for the run. A lookup that fell through to a broader scope (the usual case for a team run) is cached for CONFIG_CACHE_FALLTHROUGH_TTL_MS (5 s by default, never above the full window, 0 disables) rather than the full window, so a narrower row inserted later is seen within seconds.
concepts.title: Snapshots ≠ total immutability

concepts.body: Temporal persists execution history; PostgreSQL persists application state and searchable evidence.
concepts.detail: WorkflowRun/Step/Trace are a projection used by API/dashboard; ActiveWorkflow tracks engineering status and spend. Those records are not a replacement for Temporal history.
concepts.title: Two persistence planes

concepts.body: A policy decision records permission to proceed; another activity writes the outcome.
concepts.detail: publishOutcome returns auto/require_approval and approverCount. The template must route that result, and writeOutcome checks the latest decision. A direct runTool write is a separate path.
concepts.title: Decision ≠ side effect

concepts.body: Signals measure specific axes; passing one does not guarantee the task is correct.
concepts.detail: Online EvalResult rows include gates, review, merge, judge, trajectory, policy and PII. The offline harness compares paired golden-test outcomes and treats infrastructure errors separately.
concepts.title: Score ≠ correctness proof

concepts.body: A trusted signature proves publisher/content integrity, not safe execution or correct prompts.
concepts.detail: Install validates hash/schema and trust policy; skills and agents still require local verification. References to deployment-local MCP IDs may need rewiring. A bundle may declare dependencies only on git_repo and mcp connection types; the server refuses an install naming another, and the SDK’s validator applies the same list so an author learns it before shipping. An agent may carry its runtime: a harness runtime with a non-Anthropic model of its own is refused, an install shows a warning for each agent it moves onto the harness, and a bundle that omits the runtime leaves an installed agent’s runtime as it was.
concepts.title: Trust ≠ verification of behavior

concepts.body: Every automation decision is a row that outlives the automation, the connection and often the run.
concepts.detail: AutomationFire records one decision about one occurrence. An event automation’s rows are keyed on the repository (host/owner/repo, lowercased), not on the automation or its repository row, and the guards read that repository’s whole ledger for the source: deleting and recreating an automation cannot forget what was done, and two automations matching two workflows that fail on one push cannot open two fixes. Four keys do the work: dedupeKey names the occurrence on its host (a redelivery is decided once), subjectKey is what one run is enough for (a commit, an issue), scopeKey is what cooldown and in-flight count over (a branch, an issue), and producedKey is what a run produced (a pushed fix commit), matched by itself so a renamed repository still recognises its own output. A schedule fire and a template webhook call write rows of their own into the same table, best-effort and without a repository key, so the Automations page can say what came of each; no event guard reads them. The daily prune deletes rows that started no run once past retention and keeps STARTED rows and any row with a producedKey.
concepts.title: Decision ledger ≠ run history

features.body: Execute versioned JSON graphs on Temporal, including bounded loops, signals, parallel branches and human pauses.
features.detail: The shared interpreter owns graph semantics; RunnableWorkflow supplies activity dispatch, signal waits, persistence and cancellation. A graph is not necessarily acyclic. A graph failure ends the run once, as a non-retryable WORKFLOW_SPEC_FAILED. A cancellation of the whole run bypasses onError, onFail and onBranchFail and ends the run CANCELLED, even inside a fan-out branch. A node’s retries stop at a failure the activity marks non-retryable, after which its onFail mode decides. These paths are patched, so older histories replay the earlier behaviour.
features.title: Durable workflow graphs

features.body: Create, version, activate, import, export, compare and run reusable workflow templates.
features.detail: A template declares an input contract and workspace provider. The dashboard offers an editor and an outline view; nodes may carry optional group and title labels for display. The API validates node edges and references, refuses wait and human-step timeouts that are not positive durations, and flags context write paths through reserved segments (__proto__, prototype, constructor); a draft with such errors can be saved but not promoted, activated or used as an experiment arm. Generated versions require review before activation. When a template’s workspace provider needs a target connection that its inputs do not declare, the launch form shows a connection picker and will not submit without a choice. In the library list a workflow that cannot run shows a disabled Run with the reason (activate a draft, or promote a version). In the editor, Check workflow asks the gateway (team lead or above) to run the checks a save runs, as data: the strict parse, lint, whether the referenced agents and MCP connections exist, and the shell-authoring role and image allowlist for the template’s team. It writes no template, version or audit row and never executes the workflow, and the editor merges those findings with its own live lint, saying so when the server check could not run. It is a preview, not a promise that a save succeeds: it judges the spec alone, so it does not reproduce a save’s name checks (RESERVED_TEMPLATE_NAME, NAME_CONFLICT) or its VERSION_CONFLICT, and a result belongs to the spec at the click and is hidden once the spec is edited. Selecting a node shows collapsed help for its type (what it does, when to use it, a gotcha, a JSON example), the palette shows only the type’s what and when on hover or focus; a node whose type this build does not know is drawn as unknown instead of breaking the canvas. The save confirmation counts shell, container-step and shell-category step nodes, the same set the gateway gates on a save by the shell-authoring rule (an admin, or a team admin who is also a lead).
features.title: Workflow library & visual authoring

features.body: Generate draft workflow specs from a description and explain existing specs.
features.detail: Generation is an activity, not arbitrary runtime code execution. Slack can draft and refine team-owned versions; a person activates them.
features.title: Natural-language workflow authoring

features.body: Agent identity, model, runtime, prompt, skills, tool keys and optional MCP connection are data.
features.detail: Template → channel → team → organization → global resolution selects the most-specific active version. GLOBAL lineage pins are frozen at run start; scoped overrides remain live. Skill text is pinned separately, by revision. A team member can list only the keys, names and models an override may name, without prompts, tools or connections; the full team library stays team-admin or ADMIN. In the library table an admin sees a No credential badge on a platform-wide agent that is not pinned to its own credential and whose provider the setup readiness check marks as lacking a credential an agent can use (none reachable, or a custom provider’s credential without an apiBase; a mispinned embedding model does not make its provider count as lacking one; a sub-role persona takes its parent’s status); team, organization and template overrides are never badged. A version may set its runtime (the Mastra loop or the Claude Code harness); only a platform ADMIN can set or change it, and the library form shows the picker only on the platform-admin page. Saving the harness runtime is refused when the version’s own model, or the model it inherits along the platform-wide chain, is not Anthropic; saving a model that harness agents inherit is allowed and lists them. A new scoped override that names no runtime starts on the platform-wide row’s, which a team admin may restate but not change, unless the harness cannot drive the override’s own model. Restoring a version restores its runtime, and a seeded default-model move keeps it. An agent pinned to its own credential shows that credential’s provider and last four characters instead. Saving requires a <provider>/<model-id> spec and stores the provider lowercased; an empty string still clears the model. A credential pin is checked at save: it must exist, be for the provider the model routes to, and be reachable from the agent’s scope (a team agent may pin a GLOBAL credential, its team’s, or its team’s organization’s; an organization agent a GLOBAL one or its own organization’s), otherwise the save answers 400 INVALID_CREDENTIAL. The response carries advisory catalog and credential warnings that the dashboard shows after create, edit and restore on the platform and team libraries; an inheriting agent’s pin is not provider-checked, and a platform-wide, channel or template agent’s pin is not scope-checked at save (the worker falls back to the cascade at run time); a model with no reachable credential, or a custom provider whose reachable credentials lack an apiBase, saves with a warning rather than a refusal.
features.title: Versioned agent library

features.body: Run a launchable library agent in a throwaway repository workspace, optionally publishing a branch or draft PR.
features.detail: Separate from the engineering template. The agent runs on the Mastra loop unless its own runtime is claude-code. Step and wall-clock caps and admission limits apply. On Mastra the run is debited per step. On the harness it is one turn capped at the step ceiling: the budget is checked before the turn, each model call is debited with the budget re-checked after every debit, the wall-clock deadline stops the turn rather than failing it, toolKeys grant only the named workspace tools (none set gives the read-only tools, an empty list gives none), and its MCP connection, if it binds one, is relayed from the worker. A runtime no harness serves, or a model the harness cannot drive, is refused before any container is created. Delivery uses a fresh trusted container. A draft pull request it opens is recorded as a PullRequest row on the run’s own ledger row; a failed write appears as a pr.record_failed event on the run. No-delivery diffs are explicitly unverified. A launch may name a base branch (the CLI’s --base, or baseBranch in the request): it must be a valid branch name and not one of the platform’s own work branches, and the checkout is cut from it and the draft pull request opens into it; unset, the repository’s default branch is used.
features.title: One-off repository agent runs

features.body: Validate context, implement with test feedback, review, fix CI failures, wait for human merge and learn.
features.detail: The default spec repeats review after CI fixes. Its CI wait can use webhook signals or active polling; human merge is an external signal, not an automatic merge. An agent’s own runtime, inherited along its model chain so the fixers follow the implementer, else the run-pinned workspace.implementerRuntime setting, chooses whether implementer, fixer and merge-conflict turns run the platform’s Mastra tool loop or the Claude Code harness inside the workspace, and the run pins each agent’s choice when it starts; under the harness a worker-side policy decides every tool call, within the tools the agent’s toolKeys grant. A reviewer closing the run’s pull request unmerged makes a later push step fail non-retryably rather than open a replacement.
features.title: Ticket-to-PR engineering

features.body: Lint, typecheck, tests, build, vulnerability scan and performance benchmark activities.
features.detail: Gate commands resolve through step configuration and repository configuration. Graph failure modes can block, warn or retry; having a registered gate does not mean every template runs it.
features.title: Configurable quality gates

features.body: Split work, execute bounded fan-out branches, aggregate outputs, merge branches and resolve conflicts.
features.detail: Branch contexts are isolated and results are structured; decomposer output that fails its schema falls back to one subtask. Cross-repo epics are separate Temporal child workflows: each repository starts once its own dependencies have succeeded, and a failed upstream skips its dependents. The planner chooses order, not scope: every requested repository is in the plan, and an epic with nothing to plan fails with EPIC_PLAN_EMPTY.
features.title: Decomposition & parallel implementation

features.body: Enrich agent prompts with past lessons, tracker/knowledge content, Figma summaries and repository dependency context.
features.detail: The dependency graph supports manifest detection plus inference; upstream checkout is optional. Context helpers generally degrade on enrichment failures rather than blocking core implementation. The tracker and knowledge-base fetches check their base URL and handle redirects as described in the connector guard card.
features.title: Repository & design context

features.body: Approval, decision, input form and editable review nodes pause a run until response or timeout.
features.detail: WorkflowHumanStep stores context, deadlines and response data. HumanApproval supports distinct-approver counting. Workflow status remains RUNNING while it waits. When a step was announced in Slack, fully resolving it through the REST route (the web inbox and other API clients) or Slack edits that message to show the decision and any note and drops its buttons. The edit is best effort and never undoes the recorded answer: a Slack error is logged, while a missing bot token or an unreadable stored message skips the edit silently. In Slack, a button for a decision option resolves the step in one click, while Approve and Reject open a modal for a note first. Opening it looks the step up among the steps the clicker may act on, tells a user whose Slack id is not linked to an account to link it, and tells the clicker to use the inbox if Slack cannot open the form. The submission is what resolves the step, through the same resolve core as the REST route, which checks access again. The modal’s private metadata round-trips through the client, so it carries the step, action and Slack user under an HMAC made with the Slack signing secret, and a submission whose signature fails or whose Slack user differs is refused, with the error shown in the form. For an approval step a rejection needs a reason of at least five characters after trimming, enforced in that shared core for the web inbox, the API and Slack alike: the REST route answers 400 REASON_REQUIRED and the Slack modal shows the error in the form. An approver’s comment is optional, recorded with the response and shown, but never sent to the workflow in the signal. The REST list of steps shows pending steps by default, so resolved answers need status=ALL; actionable narrows it to pending, unexpired steps the caller may answer and has not yet answered, and answeredByMe (with status=ALL, or it finds only pending steps the caller has approved) to steps the caller resolved or approved. limit and offset page the list, and a total is counted and returned in meta only when one of those three is asked for. myResponse is the caller’s own answer: their approval row, else the stored action when they resolved the step, and null for a step resolved by a timeout or by someone else.
features.title: Four human interaction types

features.body: Classify an action by risk and choose automatic publication or human approval.
features.detail: publishOutcome records a decision; templates route it to approval. writeOutcome refuses a pending required approval. This is not a universal interceptor on every external write or MCP call.
features.title: Policy-gated outcome publication

features.body: Sensitive-file, shell-command, content, diff, skill/LLM-output, memory-content, CI-log and PII-related scanning paths.
features.detail: A skill’s description and text, an agent’s system prompt (on create and on a version that sets one) and an eval rubric’s text (on create) are scanned in full, advisorily, as are skills in a bundle install and a skill import. A pattern that overran or is quarantined, a scanner that fails, or a pattern set that cannot be read yields a scan-incomplete warning, never a clean result. Some checks block tool calls; others only annotate findings. The memory gate is blocking but INJECTION-only (a slow or quarantined EXFILTRATION pattern cannot stop a memory write): it refuses a memory write that matches or whose INJECTION scan did not complete, fails a lesson step when no pattern could be loaded, and drops a recalled item that matches. CI log text is a further consumer of the INJECTION patterns only, and only in the CI triage template (the default graph’s CI fix does not screen logs): there the log tail given to the triager is redacted for common token shapes and screened with the INJECTION patterns except template-injection (which ordinary build output matches), and a log that matches, or whose scan did not complete, is diagnosed but never fixed from. Administrator regexes execute in a budgeted worker thread. Scanning is defense-in-depth, not proof that generated code is safe. An administrator can try a candidate pattern against pasted samples before saving it: the test route validates it as a create does, then runs it through the same budgeted executor one sample at a time, writes no pattern or audit row, and neither skips a quarantined rule nor quarantines the one under test. It stops starting samples once about three budgets of wall-clock time have passed, which includes time queued behind the gateway’s other scans (the rest are reported not run), and it runs under the gateway process’s budget and reports only the first match in each sample. A sample is run as one piece of text, so the tester does not reproduce the code-security scanner’s per-line scan or the shell scanner’s segment windows and collapsed spelling; it shows whether a regex matches, not what a scanner would do with the result.
features.title: Layered runtime scanning

features.body: Run allowlisted images as shell steps or structured stdout, NDJSON or HTTP-sidecar contracts.
features.detail: Ephemeral containers default to no network, read-only root, dropped capabilities and CPU/memory/PID limits. The workspace volume is writable; opt-in egress filtering is DNS-based, not an IP firewall.
features.title: Shell & container-contract extensions

features.body: Call a named remote tool from a workflow or attach an MCP server toolset to an enabled agent.
features.detail: Generic agent nodes acquire local workspace tools only in a checkout (workspace: true); they may receive MCP tools. Enabling a connection type in the generic registry does not imply readSource/writeOutcome implements it. A connection may carry one bearer token, stored in the connection’s encrypted envelope columns and write-only: responses say only whether one is set, and audit rows record a boolean. With a token, the Authorization: Bearer header is attached only to requests for the server’s own origin and stripped from any other, the client is also pinned to the connection’s host, a redirect is refused, and the token is removed from connect error text. A connection may also carry up to five custom request headers (an API-gateway key, a tenant id): sealed together as one encrypted envelope that key rotation also covers, and write-only like the token, since responses list the header names and whether the set is unreadable and audit rows record names only. Names must be HTTP tokens and unique ignoring case, values visible ASCII (inner spaces allowed) with no line breaks and at most 2,048 characters. Authorization (the bearer token is where that credential lives), hop-by-hop headers, Host, Content-Length, Content-Type, Accept, Cookie, Set-Cookie, proxy-* headers and the MCP protocol headers are refused. Headers follow the token’s origin-only path on both transports, never overwrite a header the transport sets, and are removed from a request aimed at another origin. The connection test sends them too, with protocol and token headers taking precedence, and when headers are set its 401/403 message names the credentials in general rather than only the token. A stored set is re-validated when it is opened, so a row written by anything but the gateway route cannot put a forbidden header on the wire. A token or header set that cannot be decrypted yields no agent tools and makes an mcp workflow node fail, rather than connecting without what the server expects. Pointing a connection at another origin while keeping its stored token is refused with 409 TOKEN_ORIGIN_CHANGE, and keeping stored header values while changing the origin is refused with 409 HEADERS_ORIGIN_CHANGE. An unreadable header set can only be replaced or removed (409 HEADERS_UNREADABLE otherwise). The token and headers belong to the connection, so every run that uses it presents the same credentials, not the launching user’s. An ADMIN may also turn on allowPrivateNetwork for a connection. It uses the same guard as the tracker and knowledge-base connectors: with it on, a server on a private address is accepted when the connection is saved, when it is tested, and each time the worker loads its tools. Loopback, link-local, cloud-metadata addresses and names, unspecified and malformed addresses and non-http(s) schemes are refused whatever the flag says. The flag is part of the connection’s saved configuration and every save re-checks the URL against the flag sent with it, so an update to a private-address server that does not send the flag is refused with 400 UNSAFE_URL. Every request the worker makes to an MCP server, with or without credentials, is resolved and pinned, and the opt-in covers only the connection’s own origin, so an SSE endpoint or redirect on another origin is strict. With a token or headers a redirect is refused; without them redirects are followed by hand, at most three hops, each hop text-checked and pinned, with MCP session headers kept for the server’s own origin and only a benign allowlist crossing to another. The admin connection test resolves and pins with the connection’s opt-in, never follows a redirect, and reports a refused resolution as an address on a network the connection may not reach. The admin connection test lists tools with the stored token, using streamable HTTP and falling back to the legacy SSE transport after a failure that another transport might fix; a URL ending /sse goes straight to SSE. Under the Claude Code harness the agent’s connection is relayed from the worker: the worker connects with the connection’s credentials and guard and serves its tools to the harness through an in-process MCP server over the SDK’s pipe, so the credentials never enter the container. The policy allows exactly those tools, and the harness loads no other MCP server (a repository’s .mcp.json included).
features.title: MCP as nodes and agent tools

features.body: Let MCP clients list repositories, work requests, runs and pending human steps, and optionally submit work or cancel runs as the signed-in user.
features.detail: A stateless Streamable HTTP endpoint is an OAuth 2.1 resource server; better-auth issues tokens after a consent screen, and users can revoke connected apps. Off by default, and write scope needs a second switch. Tools reach data only through the REST routes, so route authorization applies; writes add a per-user rate limit, a budget-tier allowlist, a required idempotency key and a concurrent-run cap.
features.title: MCP server for external agents

features.body: Reply in threads, launch durable tasks, draft workflows and maintain channel memory.
features.detail: Opt-in capabilities include follow-up sessions, reactive interjections, ambient digests, passive ingestion, open-item nudges and organization signal flagging. Proactivity has cooldowns and budgets. When a task cannot start, or its thread already has one running, the thread is told so instead of receiving the agent’s acknowledgement.
features.title: Channel-resident Slack assistants

features.body: Store lessons and channel memory with run/agent lineage and evidence; recall them for every agent that works on a repository; supersede, consolidate and forget them through their provenance.
features.detail: MemoryItem supports generic scopes and entities plus repo/channel/team/org links. Storage uses vector(1536); a row is compared only with rows embedded by the same model, and after a model change an admin starts a re-embed of the stale rows. Scoped searches set pgvector's iterative index scan (strict order), so a small repository beside a crowded one still gets its nearest rows; on pgvector before 0.8 the worker logs once and searches without it. Every built-in engineering template with a review or CI loop writes a lesson when that loop runs out of attempts, and default-engineering also after a merge and after a merge-wait timeout that followed a rejection; the release templates and the four-eyes sign-off loop write none, and a step that throws writes none. commitToMemory is given bounded evidence chosen by outcome (a CI failure lesson gets the CI log, a review failure lesson the rejection), records the outcome by code, cites the pull requests, head commit and a short quote of that evidence, and grades its confidence; a low-confidence lesson is labelled on recall, not filtered. It also rebuilds the run's earlier review rejections and CI failures from its traces — grouped by Temporal activity id so a retry counts once, capped at five entries and 4,000 characters per kind — and fences them with the evidence. A new item at or above memory.supersedeThreshold similarity to older active items in the same repository or channel marks them superseded; they are kept but not recalled. Consolidation soft-deletes merged items and keeps the sources' ids. An optional memory.lessonMaxAgeDays setting (off by default) keeps older lessons out of recall, searchLessons and consolidation through a SQL filter before the limit; nothing is deleted. The implementer, the three fixers and the review personas recall their repository's lessons by the text of what they are working on, and the Mastra loop also gets read-only searchLessons and explainLesson tools bound to that repository. Deleting a lesson or channel item forgets every merged copy of it and a merged item's own sources, restores the rows only the deleted merge or supersession hid, and audits both id lists in the same transaction; an API-only admin route erases one Slack user's attributed channel memory the same way. Recalled memory is text a later run reads, so the worker gates it on injection patterns: a write through insertMemoryItem is refused before it is embedded when its lesson or rationale matches an INJECTION scanner pattern, and the two consolidation passes apply the same check to their merged notes before inserting, leaving the cluster as it was. Lesson and channel-memory retrieval drop any recalled item that matches, which also covers rows written before the gate and an admin’s edit: PATCH /slack-channels/:id/memory/:memoryId saves edited text without the check. A write is refused when its INJECTION scan is incomplete (a pattern overran its budget or is quarantined), and the two consolidation passes treat an incomplete, failed or unloadable scan the same way and leave the cluster as it was. A pattern set that cannot be read is different, because no rule ran: the lesson step fails and is retried (bounded; a lesson is lost if the outage outlasts the retries), while a direct lesson write is logged and dropped and a channel turn’s summary or passively ingested fact is not stored. Recall gates only on the patterns that ran, so an incomplete scan alone drops nothing; a scan that throws, or a pattern set that cannot be loaded, recalls nothing, and a lesson’s explanation is then withheld as could-not-be-scanned rather than as an injection match. Every prompt that carries memory — recalled lessons, and channel memory in a mention turn, a reactive interjection, an ambient digest and both lists of an org-flagging check — wraps it in a block that labels the notes reference data, not instructions. The gate does not use the EXFILTRATION patterns, and passing the gate is not proof that recalled text is benign. A shell step’s command text is masked for credential-shaped values before it becomes an auto-commit message or a stored lesson. The lessons routes list and delete only repository lessons (scope swe-lessons), not channel memory, and a lesson delete writes an audit row carrying the deleted content.
features.title: Scoped semantic memory

features.body: Capture online signals, score workflow values, compare candidates to baselines and revalidate datasets.
features.detail: Hard floors are gate/assert/policy/PII. Trajectory and judge scores are soft by default; a judge call records its model and cost on the result row. A dataset run shares a runless token cap scaled by its case count and ends with a partial verdict when that cap, or its organization’s monthly USD cap, stops it after a case completed; the verdict records which, and run lists label it partial. Frozen fixture SHAs, golden tests, rubric versions and quarantined cases support reproducible comparisons. Admins can follow per-scorer trends over a 7, 30 or 90 day window or a custom range of whole UTC days (at most 366, bucketed by week above 90 days), split by judge model, agent or implementer runtime and filtered to the results of one template’s runs, and see each dataset’s quarantined share of golden cases against its ceiling. Each case resolves its settings and Agent rows in the dataset’s team and organization scope. An eval run started through the API or CLI can name a runtime (Mastra loop or Claude Code harness) for either side; it applies as that case’s per-agent runtime pin and workspace.implementerRuntime pin, so it wins over the Agent’s own runtime, and a case whose runner is built on a different runtime fails with EVAL_RUNTIME_MISMATCH instead of being graded. A side without an override resolves its runtime per case, since an eval has no run to pin it on. Each harness result row records the candidate’s runtime, with the baseline’s in its metadata, and the run summary lists the runtimes each side ran on; the run pages, results table and CLI show them, and the dashboard does not start runs.
features.title: Evaluation & regression system

features.body: Route runs between template versions and track agent canary/control outcomes.
features.detail: This is evaluation/routing metadata. It differs from the canary-rollout template, which waits for external staging and monitoring signals.
features.title: Experiments and canaries

features.body: Track tokens and catalog-priced USD across runs, runless workflows, teams, organizations and Slack channels, and stop a capped organization’s spend at launch and before each model call.
features.detail: Token tiers bind runs; a workflow with no run has a per-execution token cap. The organization USD cap is checked at launch and again before every budgeted model call, which refuses with a non-retryable BUDGET_EXCEEDED naming the organization. Both read finalized, in-flight and runless spend; the mid-run read goes through a per-organization cache of one config window. One rule, billedOrgId, places a run for the in-flight count, the mid-run guard and finalization billing: the work request’s connection, else the run’s own connection, else the repository of its own ledger row, and the first source that exists decides. A scheduled fire gets its own ledger row and run connection from its schedule’s repository, and epic planning declares the first repository’s team as its spend owner, so neither sits outside the cap. A scheduled run reaper finalizes and bills runs whose workflow ended without finalizing them. Prompt-cache reads and writes are priced at cache rates: a model’s catalog row may set read, 5-minute-write and 1-hour-write multipliers, each falling back to the code table, where Anthropic 1-hour writes cost twice input. Each trace row records its owning team and organization, which drives per-team and per-org usage reports: ADMINs see everything, a team LEAD their team, an ORG_ADMIN their organization, and the usage page opens for anyone who holds at least one of those scopes rather than by platform role. A model with no catalog price is refused when the organization its run bills to has a monthly USD cap (resolved by the same billedOrgId rule as the cap, so a PRD run or a code-route channel task counts through its connection), when a runless workflow’s spend owner is a capped organization, and when the call belongs to a channel with a monthly cap; a repo-less channel task bills its channel, so only the channel cap refuses it. Anywhere else it is recorded at zero USD with token usage retained. The usage report and the workflow-template analytics accept a custom since/until range of whole UTC days (at most 366, not in the future) in place of the preset window; the usage series is bucketed by week above 90 days. The 7, 30 and 90 day presets on the usage report and the workflow-template analytics likewise cover whole UTC days ending with today, so a preset spans the days a custom range of that length would and its previous period is the equal-length span directly before it.
features.title: Cost, budgets & usage

features.body: Inspect node attempts, tool calls, LLM responses, artifacts, policy decisions and telemetry.
features.detail: PostgreSQL is the queryable application ledger; Temporal owns durable execution history. OpenTelemetry loads as a preload so HTTP is instrumented, and trace context travels in Temporal headers, so a gateway request and every activity of the run it starts share a trace without OpenTelemetry code in the workflow isolate. A run started by a schedule has no starting context, so the workflow interceptor derives one from the workflow id and first run id and its activities share that trace. The gateway stamps its signals and updates with the caller’s context, and activities scheduled after one carry a span link to it. Trace rows link to their spec node and span; an agent’s tool calls are recorded as they execute, with real durations, and survive a generate call that later throws. Worker logs, gateway logs and the bash, MCP and harness audit lines written inside an activity export over OTLP with trace context. The run page tails new rows, reconciles by count and asks for the spec snapshot only once. Large outputs can be offloaded to PostgreSQL or S3-compatible artifacts.
features.title: Run and agent observability

features.body: Scope resources by organization/team, share repositories with teams and apply role-based permissions.
features.detail: Repository reachability combines ownership/sharing with optional host-permission checks. Per-user credentials are bound to their verified origins and the current run launcher. Query guards supplement route-specific authorization. A repository on another approved GitHub host is reached only with that host’s own credentials or the launcher’s own token, never the instance’s; with neither, the run is refused (see per-host GitHub credentials). A team’s own page also lists the repositories shared with it (sharedRepositories on GET /teams/:id), read-only, active rows only, and under an enforcing repo-access gate only those the caller’s own GitHub permission reaches; a platform ADMIN is not gated.
features.title: Organizations, teams & repository access

features.body: Filter and page the configuration audit log and runtime security events.
features.detail: Audit rows name actors by email, and a deleted actor keeps its id. Security events page on the server. A separate summary route returns per-type counts: all time when no window is given, otherwise for the window plus the equal-length window before it. The dashboard always sends its selected date range (30 days by default), shows each count against the previous window, and filters the list when a type is selected. Both views are ADMIN-only. The audit search box matches the actor’s email or name and the entity type as substrings; an entity id (or actor id) matches only when the whole uuid is typed, because a partial id is not matched at all, and a search that matches more than 200 people considers only 200 of them. The CSV export applies the same filter as the list, writes newest first in batches, and holds at most a fixed number of rows: when more match, the response says so in a header and the dashboard tells the admin the file holds only the newest rows and states the limit, so a larger history needs narrower filters or a shorter date range. On the audit route, a WorkflowRun row also carries the id of the request it belongs to. Template, team and organization administration is recorded in the same log: template create (including a generated draft), edit, new version, promote and webhook enable or revoke; team create, update, deactivation, memberships and the shell-image and egress allowlists; organization rename and membership changes. Agent library create, version update and deletion are recorded at platform and team scope; an update entry holds the model, runtime and version before and after (the team entry also its key, scope and team), not the prompt. Refining a template into a new version, a draft saved by an asynchronous generation job, and the review mark that gates promoting an AI-generated version write no audit row. A template entry holds identity, status, version and routing fields, never the spec text, and a webhook entry records only whether one exists, never the token. Template, team, organization and agent entries are written after the change as a separate statement, not in its transaction, so a failed audit insert errors after the change has applied.
features.title: Audit and security-event review

features.body: Launch scheduled repository work, template webhook calls and GitHub-event automations, and run maintenance sweeps.
features.detail: Temporal schedules also drive eval regression/revalidation, lesson consolidation, repository dependency scans and permission sync. Some jobs are off by default and need explicit operator configuration (repository access sync, eval regression and revalidation); lesson consolidation, repository dependency scans, provider model discovery, the run reaper, the skill-source update check and the automation-decision prune, by contrast, are on by default. The schedule settings are read at gateway startup, and the system-wide schedules are synchronized once the gateway’s Temporal connection is up, which may be later than boot (see the gateway-without-Temporal card). Schedules of a Slack channel or a scheduled work request are reconciled when their own rows are written, not at startup, and a write that needs one is refused with 503 TEMPORAL_UNAVAILABLE until the gateway’s first connection. After that connection a Slack channel write stands when its schedule sync fails (logged) and a channel delete tears its schedules down best-effort, while a scheduled work request syncs Temporal first or rolls its rows back. The scheduled-work list reports exists: null with unavailable: true for a schedule whose live state could not be asked, which differs from exists: false. Edits to a scheduled work request are compare-and-set on a row version and retry a few times when a competing write changed only the acting user or fire bookkeeping; any other competing change is a 409. When a repository share is removed or the repository moves, each schedule of a team left with no claim is deactivated and audited on its own (the acting user is the actor), before its Temporal schedule is paused; an audit failure is logged and does not skip the pause. The run reaper is one system-wide schedule (every 15 minutes by default) that finalizes runs whose Temporal execution is over; it is paused, not removed, when disabled. The skill-source check is one system-wide schedule (daily by default) that asks each tracked source’s host which commit its ref names and only flags a different one; it is paused, not removed, when disabled. A scheduled fire is a run like any other for budgets: it gets a ledger row and run connection at its first activity, and the pull request it opens links to that execution’s own ledger row so CI signals reach the right workflow. While a re-run (or any other non-fire run) of a schedule’s standing request is in flight, each fire is skipped as a refused execution with reason request-in-flight, logged at info and audited (event fire-skipped, action UPDATE) at most once an hour, and the schedule resumes on the first tick after the run ends. A re-run is refused with 409 WORKFLOW_ALREADY_EXISTS while any live ledger row of the request exists: a fire’s, an earlier run’s, or a child run that carries the request’s id. Both read the request’s non-terminal ledger rows, the schedule’s anchor excluded, and confirm each with Temporal before refusing: a finished or absent workflow has its stale row closed with the status Temporal reports (COMPLETED, TIMED_OUT, CANCELLED for terminated or cancelled, else FAILED) and does not block (closing the row is best-effort: a failed close is ignored and the next check asks again), a row written in the last five minutes is trusted, and when Temporal cannot be asked or does not answer within three seconds the row blocks and the refusal says so. The re-run also confirms the row its workflow id allocator refuses on, which reads only the ticket’s eng- family and never asks Temporal itself, and allocates again once that row is closed. A run ended by a SKIPPED terminate node closes its ledger row as COMPLETED, so it never reads as in flight. Between the read and the start there is no lock. The automation-decision prune is one system-wide schedule (daily at 04:37 by default; AUTOMATION_DECISION_PRUNE_ENABLED and AUTOMATION_DECISION_PRUNE_CRON, read when the schedules sync once Temporal connects) that deletes decision-ledger rows which started no run once they are older than workflow.automationDecisionRetentionDays (90 days by default, at least 7, GLOBAL scope only); it is paused, not removed, when disabled. Rows that started a run, and rows naming a commit the platform produced, are never deleted. A scheduled fire and a template webhook call also leave a row in that ledger (started, or refused with a reason, a refusal recorded once an hour per reason) so the Automations page can say what came of each; recording is best-effort and never fails the fire or the call, and no event-source guard reads these rows.
features.title: Scheduled automation & webhooks

features.body: The gateway starts and serves while Temporal is unreachable, connecting in the background; routes that need a workflow client answer a retryable 503.
features.detail: The Temporal plugin registers at once and retries the connection with a doubling delay from one second up to thirty, logging the first attempts at warn and later ones at debug. Until the first connection succeeds, every call through the gateway’s Temporal helpers raises a dedicated error. Where a route does not handle it, the global handler answers 503 with the code TEMPORAL_UNAVAILABLE and a Retry-After of five seconds (logged at warn, not error); routes that handle Temporal failures keep their own answers (the GitHub webhook signal paths answer 503 SIGNAL_FAILED, an event-automation delivery whose run could not be started after three attempts answers 503 AUTOMATION_START_FAILED so the delivery can be sent again, Slack shows a temporarily-unavailable message, and the scheduled-work list degrades). That error is not a workflow-not-found error: callers that signal or look up a workflow treat it as could-not-confirm, roll back and ask for a retry. Routes that would persist a row whose consistency depends on a Temporal call check the connection first and refuse before writing: eval launches (so an outage is not recorded as a failed eval), Slack channel registration with a digest or poll, a change to a Slack channel’s active flag, digest or poll enablement or cron, and channel deletion (an edit that leaves those values as stored goes through), and the saves of system settings that synchronize a schedule. The Slack approval path answers a temporarily-unavailable message. A channel knowledge edit’s re-embedding is deliberately not gated on Temporal. System-wide Temporal schedules (lesson consolidation, repository dependency scan, permission sync, model discovery, run reaper, skill-source check, automation-decision prune, eval regression and revalidation) are synchronized once the connection comes up, each best-effort: a failure is logged. Only consolidation, eval regression and revalidation have an admin save route that re-syncs them; the environment-driven ones (repository dependency scan, repository access sync, model discovery, run reaper, skill-source check, automation-decision prune) are next synced at the following gateway start. GET /health always answers 200 with status ok while the process serves requests and adds temporal: connecting or connected, so a container healthcheck keyed on it does not depend on Temporal. The per-client request limit is read once at boot from RATE_LIMIT_MAX (default 200) and RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_SECONDS (default 60); a value that is not a positive integer fails the boot instead of falling back to the default.
features.title: Gateway boots without Temporal

features.body: The dashboard lists work by request, with the latest visible attempt standing for each, and retries a request without losing its identity.
features.detail: Run visibility is applied first, then executions are grouped by request. A single-repository request is represented by its newest visible execution; a cross-repository request summarizes every visible child and keeps failed children visible while others run. Filtering and paging happen after grouping, so an old failure cannot resurface behind a successful retry. A retry starts a new execution of the same request from its recorded template version. Whether the request targeted a repository or not, it applies the template checks a fresh launch applies (the template must be ACTIVE and visible through the caller’s team membership, a recorded input is validated against its input schema); a repository request additionally re-checks repository access, and a connection-free or non-repository one re-checks the connection and the organization budget. An agent re-run reuses the request id with a fresh delivery branch. Optional instructions are appended to the new attempt’s description only. A cross-repository request is not retried as a whole.
features.title: Request-centred work inbox and retry

features.body: Read and write Notion pages, Zendesk comments, tracker issues and Slack messages.
features.detail: These have concrete worker connectors. HubSpot and generic http_api branches in genericActions currently return placeholders. MCP has its own executor instead. Their requests either refuse redirects (Notion, Zendesk, Slack and Linear; Jira treats a 3xx as a failure) or, for GitHub Issues, re-check every hop through a guarded fetch, so a credential cannot leave the configured origin.
features.title: Non-engineering API handlers

features.body: Connector requests to tracker and knowledge-base base URLs, and MCP server URLs, pass a text check and a connection-time resolve-and-pin check whose private-network opt-in is narrow, and connector requests refuse or re-check every redirect.
features.detail: Jira, GitHub Issues and Confluence base URLs are checked strictly first when those connectors run, and Jira field detection, an ADMIN call, runs the same check before it builds its client and answers 400 BASE_URL_REFUSED for a refused URL, whether it came from the stored row or the environment fallback. Only when that check refuses a private address and the connector’s allowPrivateNetwork opt-in is on is the refusal waived, and the waiver is logged. The same opt-in decides whether a resolved private address is accepted when the request connects (see the resolve-and-pin card). MCP connections use the same address check, with the flag stored on each connection (see the MCP card): every MCP save re-checks the URL, and the waiver is recorded in the audit trail rather than logged. A refused loopback, link-local or unspecified address is reported as such, with or without the opt-in, rather than as a private-network refusal that would suggest the opt-in could help. The opt-in never reaches loopback, link-local (IPv4 and IPv6), cloud-metadata or unspecified addresses, multicast or the reserved and documentation ranges, nor a malformed URL or a scheme other than http(s). The worker’s Jira path honours the opt-in only for the exact origin an ADMIN configured. The tracker and knowledge-base save routes apply the same check and answer 400 BASE_URL_REFUSED for a stored target the connector would refuse, but only when the write touches the provider or URL or turns the opt-in on, so a save that only turns it off is never blocked. Redirects are never followed unchecked. Linear, Notion, Slack, Zendesk and Figma requests set redirect: error, and the Atlassian client treats any 3xx as a failure it does not retry. GitHub Issues and the CI-log download, which GitHub answers with redirects, go through a guarded fetch: redirects are followed by hand for at most three hops, the guard runs on every hop, the credential is sent only to the configured origin, only a short allowlist of benign headers crosses to another origin, a write cannot cross origins, a 307 or 308 keeps the method and body, and every hop is also resolved and pinned. GitHub Issues waives private addresses only on its configured origin. The CI-log download waives them only on the credential’s and the repository’s GitHub origins, except for a repository on a GitHub Enterprise host (any web or API base other than github.com), where every hop of the download may resolve to a private address because its log storage usually sits on the same network; the token still goes only to the log URL’s origin. Figma has no opt-in: its host is a constant that is still run through the guard. The tracker, knowledge-base and Figma connection tests also accept unsaved form values. A blank token means the stored one, but a typed provider or base URL that differs from the saved one (for Notion, whose address is fixed, only a different provider counts) is refused unless the token is typed again, so a stored token is not sent to a target it was not saved for, and such a typed URL passes the guard first. Figma’s host is fixed, so a typed token can only go there. Knowledge-base test failures are fixed messages by class (credentials, not found, unreachable, failed), never text from the remote service, and the check uses a dedicated connection test that throws on a rejected credential instead of a search that returns nothing.
features.title: Connector base URLs and redirects are guarded

features.body: Requests to operator-supplied URLs resolve the host once, refuse the request if any answer is internal, and connect only to an address from that checked answer.
features.detail: The text guard reads only the URL, so a public name that resolves to an internal address passes it. createGuardedFetch closes that at connection time: it drives undici’s own fetch with a dispatcher whose connect lookup resolves the name once (bounded to 5 s), classifies every returned address with the text guard’s rules, and refuses the request if any one is refused; a resolver error, timeout or empty answer also refuses, with a fixed message. The socket is handed only addresses from that checked answer, so the check and the connection share one resolution. They are ordered IPv4 first and tried in turn with a 300 ms per-attempt wait, over HTTP/1.1 only, while TLS server name and Host stay the hostname. A literal IP never reaches the lookup, so it is classified before the request. Private ranges (RFC 1918, CGNAT, unique-local IPv6, and 198.18.0.0/15, which fake-IP proxy tools answer every name with) pass only with the call site’s opt-in. Loopback, link-local, unspecified and cloud-metadata addresses (GCP’s fd20:ce::254 and OCI’s 192.0.0.192 included), multicast, and the reserved, IETF protocol, documentation, 6to4 relay, Teredo and discard ranges never pass, whether written as a literal or returned by DNS. The call sites are bundle install-from-URL, the provider credential test, model discovery and the catalog refresh (strict unless the apiBase host is listed in models.privateNetworkHosts, which waives only the private-range refusal), the worker’s chat-model and embedding calls and the Claude Code model proxy’s upstream calls (the same listed-host rule, with redirects refused), the Jira and Confluence (Atlassian) and GitHub Issues connectors, the worker’s Jira connector, the worker’s MCP transports and the gateway’s MCP connection test, skill-source fetches, the CI-log download, and the GitHub connection test when its API URL is typed and unsaved. createOriginScopedFetch applies a private-network waiver only to named origins, which is how the MCP opt-in and the CI-log allowance cover the configured host while any other hop is strict; GitHub Issues does the same by choosing a permissive or a strict fetch per hop. A refused resolution carries the ESSRF_BLOCKED code: model discovery and the credential test report it as blocked address and the MCP test says the address resolves to a network the connection may not reach, never resolver detail. Under an environment proxy the guarded fetch dispatches through Node’s own fetch so the proxy’s routing is used; the host is still checked up front but the connection is not pinned. The repository’s invariant check fails a bare fetch (a call, a default parameter or a passed value) in the modules whose every request is operator-supplied, so an injectable fetch cannot silently default back to the text-only path.
features.title: Operator URLs are resolved and pinned at connection time

features.body: Package agents, skills, scanner patterns and templates for export/install and SDK authoring.
features.detail: Manifest v2 hashes identity and content; detached Ed25519 signatures are checked against deployment trust keys. Unverified install is denied unless allowed. Installing a skill over an existing one cuts a new revision when its text or description differs, always clears its verification, and scans it; a concurrent edit to that skill rolls back the whole install. Credentials and connection instances are not portable bundle content. An ADMIN installs a bundle inline (the CLI’s bundles install <path>, or a .json file picked or dropped in Studio) or from a URL (Studio or the CLI). The URL path text-checks every hop as public-only, resolves and pins it with no private-network opt-in, follows at most five redirects, times out after 15 s and caps the streamed body at BUNDLE_MAX_BYTES (5 MB by default); the inline preview and install routes accept a request body of that cap plus 64 KiB. Studio’s file flow parses the file in the browser (invalid JSON, a non-object or a file over the gateway’s cap — read from GET /platform/bundles/limits, 5 MB while that answer loads or is unavailable — is reported without sending anything), previews the parsed bundle and installs that same object; both install routes take an optional expectedContentHash and answer 409 BUNDLE_CHANGED when the bundle’s declared hash differs from it, and the install then re-derives the hash, so whatever the hash covers is what was previewed. Studio sends the hash on both paths; the CLI sends none and installs without a preview.
features.title: Portable signed bundles

features.body: Price models from a catalog, and on a schedule ask each provider which models it lists, storing unreviewed suggestions instead of catalog rows.
features.detail: The gateway upserts one Temporal schedule, auto-swe-model-discovery, once the Temporal connection is up; it runs ScheduledModelDiscoveryWorkflow, a single discoverModels activity that lists models through every GLOBAL provider credential. It is on by default (MODEL_DISCOVERY_ENABLED, MODEL_DISCOVERY_CRON, read when the schedule is synchronized once the Temporal connection is up); disabling pauses the schedule rather than deleting it. Results go to model_suggestions (NEW: listed but priced nowhere; RETIREMENT_CANDIDATE: a priced model missing from a complete listing) and model_discovery_provider_status, never to catalog rows, so a suggestion cannot make a model known at $0. A failed provider changes only its status row; an incomplete listing (page cap, empty result, an unfollowable continuation) still records new suggestions but deletes nothing and flags no retirement candidates; a dismissal survives refreshes; deleting a provider’s GLOBAL credential removes only the credential: the next discovery pass, scheduled or on demand, removes that provider’s suggestion and status rows, and until then the suggestions endpoint still serves them. Every failure is reduced to a fixed string (HTTP <status>, timed out, request failed (<name>, <code>; the code is omitted when absent), credential could not be decrypted, blocked address, apiBase required, unrecognised response), so no fetch or provider text reaches the status row, logs or Temporal history, and a credential save rejects a key with whitespace or control characters and an apiBase carrying a username or password. An apiBase on a private network (any provider’s) is refused on the credential Test button, model discovery and the catalog refresh (which also check every resolved address) and, as URL text only, on credential save, unless its host (or host:port, as the URL spells it) is listed in the ADMIN-only, GLOBAL-only setting models.privateNetworkHosts; the listing waives only the private-range refusal, and loopback, localhost, link-local, cloud-metadata, unspecified, multicast and reserved addresses stay refused whatever is listed. A setting that cannot be read leaves the list empty, so the strict guard applies. The list also applies to the model and embedding calls agents make, and a call to an unlisted host that resolves to a private address fails before any request is sent; those calls refuse redirects, so a provider that answers with a 30x must be pointed at its final URL. The list is read per request behind the settings cache, so a client built earlier picks up a change, and an unreadable setting leaves it empty. A built-in provider (anthropic, openai, google) with an apiBase is probed and listed at that base instead of the vendor’s, keeping the provider’s auth style (a Google probe against a custom base sends the key in x-goog-api-key, not in the URL). Because a proxy exposes aliases rather than the vendor catalog, such a listing is never marked complete: it still proposes new models but never proposes retiring one. An apiBase carrying a query or fragment is rejected for every provider, since /models would land inside it. Admins read the suggestions in the Catalog tab, where the on-demand discover route refreshes the same rows. Nothing is added to the catalog or retired automatically.
features.title: Model catalog & scheduled discovery

features.body: Reach repositories on other approved GitHub hosts with that host’s own PAT or App, and never send a platform credential to a host it does not belong to.
features.detail: GitHubHostCredential holds, per approved non-instance host family, an optional PAT and/or a GitHub App (id and private key), encrypted with the platform envelope and managed by ADMINs through routes that return only whether a secret is set and its last four characters. resolvePlatformCredential returns instance, host, mismatch, misconfigured or installation-mismatch. A launcher’s own saved token still wins; a host’s set is built from its row alone (no instance PAT, App, auth mode or singleton installation) and lapses when the host leaves github.repositoryHosts. resolveGitHubToken refuses any API host outside the set’s credentialHost as a last line, for the PAT, installation tokens and the App JWT. GitHubInstallation is identified by (host, installationId) with the host fixed at creation, and a repository may point only at an installation on its own host: checked when the repository is written and again when a run token is minted (REPO_INSTALLATION_HOST_MISMATCH), The installation’s host is required wherever a token is minted: the repository types the worker’s SCM calls and the shared mint-time check take (RepoRef, InstallationScopedRepo) declare it without an optional, so a caller that does not load it fails to compile, and a repository with an installation but no host reads as a mismatch, failing closed. GitHub’s own installation lifecycle events (installation deleted, suspend and unsuspend, and installation_target renamed) are only a prompt: the gateway confirms with GET /app/installations/{id}, signed with the App JWT of the host the delivery’s secret proved, and applies only what GitHub answers (404 is deleted, suspended_at is suspended, otherwise active; a rename updates accountLogin). A host with no App credentials, a failed lookup, or an installation nobody registered changes nothing, so a forged or replayed delivery that GitHub contradicts is harmless; installations are never created automatically. GitHubInstallation.retiredReason records that a retirement came from a webhook, so a webhook reverses only its own retirements, an admin’s isActive change clears it, and the write is conditional on the row as read. Each applied change is audited with the state GitHub confirmed. The login-ownership check reads the account a login was recorded against (users.github_login_account_id) and asks that account’s host with that host’s credential; a non-github.com host with no credential is reported unverifiable, keeping the login, and a github.com account with no applicable credential is asked unauthenticated, so the check is rate-limited. A confirmed mismatch clears the login only if it and its source account are unchanged since they were read, and records a takeover. Unlinking a GitHub account clears the login only when it is the source account.
features.title: Per-host GitHub credentials & installations

features.body: A skill’s text is an immutable revision, and a run reads the revisions it pinned at start, so editing a skill mid-run does not change what a retry or replay sees.
features.detail: Every write that changes a skill’s text or description (create, edit, boot sync, bundle install) cuts a SkillRevision in the same statement, guarded on the revision number the writer read; a concurrent edit gets 409 SKILL_CHANGED (PUT also accepts expectedRevision), and the boot sync skips a race it lost. createWorkflowRun stores {skillId: revision} in WorkflowRun.skillRevisions for every skill visible to GLOBAL plus the run’s team and organization (a repo-less channel task uses its Slack channel’s). Skill reads for agents use the pinned text, and the pin is part of the resolveAgent cache key. isActive is deliberately read live (within the config cache window of about 30 s), so an admin can switch a harmful skill off under a running run. isVerified describes the current text. An admin edit or bundle install that cuts a revision clears it, and a pinned older revision never reports as verified. For custom and bundle-installed skills, only POST /platform/skills/:id/verify (ADMIN, naming the revision, 409 when stale) sets it; the boot sync re-verifies the seeded built-ins on every start, including when it cuts a revision from shipped text. Skill descriptions and text are scanned in full on create, edit and bundle install; the scan is advisory and is marked incomplete when a pattern is quarantined or the scanner fails.
features.title: Immutable skill revisions pinned per run

features.body: An ADMIN previews skills in a GitHub or GitHub Enterprise repository, then installs the chosen ones pinned to the commit that was previewed.
features.detail: Preview writes nothing: it resolves the ref to a commit and reads each SKILL.md under the path. The install request names skills and the previewed commit, never text; the server fetches again at that commit and fails with 409 if the ref has moved. A non-github.com host must be an approved repository host, and one on a private network must also be listed in a separate setting; the platform credential for that host is the only one used, and a host with none is read anonymously. Fetches are bounded in requests, bytes, skills and time. Skills with scan warnings are refused while the blocking setting is on (it is on by default). One transaction takes a name lock, checks name conflicts across the scopes the skill would be visible in, and writes the source plus every skill at revision 1, unverified, with its source commit. Markdown and text siblings are kept as reference text unscanned and nothing is executed. Wherever a model reads an imported skill’s text, it is labelled third-party with its source and short commit while the revision it reads carries a source commit; an admin’s hand edit cuts a revision without one, which drops the label, and a deleted source drops the repository name (the label reads external@sha7). Updates to an imported source are a separate, reviewed flow: a scheduled check flags a moved ref, and an ADMIN diffs and accepts it. A preview request that names one skill returns that skill’s complete incoming text and writes nothing; it is read at the previewed commit and fails with a moved-ref conflict only when the request names that commit (the field is optional), otherwise it reads what the ref names now. The dashboard’s External sources tab drives the flow, and it is the dashboard that requires a skill’s full text to be read at the previewed commit before it can be ticked and sends only skills it read; the create and install routes take skill names and require no earlier read. Skills the pinned commit holds that nothing installed uses can be installed later. The install is read by the pinned sha and never through the ref, so upstream ref movement does not affect it, and it takes a per-source lock plus the name lock and never moves the pin. It applies the import rules (ALREADY_INSTALLED for a folder already installed, NAME_CONFLICT, scan warnings blocked by the setting), refuses STALE_SHA when the sha is not the pin, DISABLED for a source disabled before the request and 404 for one deleted before it. SOURCE_CHANGED means the source was disabled, deleted, re-pinned by an accept or switched to another script mode while the install ran. Nothing is written on any refusal. A folder first added upstream after the pin is UNKNOWN_SKILLS until an accept advances the pin. The skill list marks each skill still attached to a source with that source and the commit its current text was cut from; the commit is empty after a hand edit. In the External sources views and the skill list, repository-derived text (names, descriptions, paths, diff lines, full text) is rendered as plain text, and each control, format, line or paragraph separator and default-ignorable character is shown as a ⟨U+XXXX⟩ marker, except the variation selectors and joiners that make up an emoji and, in text bodies, newline and tab; other look-alike spaces are not marked, and the skill editor shows stored text raw. The gateway stores names, descriptions, text and diffs as parsed and does not mask them; only folder and file paths and ignored frontmatter keys pass through the display function that replaces those characters with ? and cuts to 120 characters.
features.title: Skill import from an external GitHub repository

features.body: A schedule flags when an imported source’s ref names a different commit; an ADMIN reads a per-skill diff in the dashboard or the CLI and accepts it, which cuts new skill revisions. Nothing updates on its own.
features.detail: The gateway upserts one Temporal schedule, auto-swe-skill-source-sync, once the Temporal connection is up; it runs ScheduledSkillSourceSyncWorkflow, a single syncSkillSources activity. It is on by default (SKILL_SOURCE_SYNC_ENABLED, cadence SKILL_SOURCE_SYNC_CRON, default 41 5 * * *), read from the environment at gateway start, and paused rather than removed when disabled. The sweep visits each source that is not disabled, one at a time. A check resolves the ref to a commit and fetches no tree or file. It writes only latestSha, status, lastError and lastCheckedAt, guarded on the pinned commit and on the source not being disabled, so a concurrent accept or disable wins and the check’s write is dropped. A failing source does not stop the others; when a host answers that it is rate limited, only the source that got that answer has its check time moved; the host’s remaining sources are not asked and nothing is written for them until the next run. The same check runs on demand for one source. The diff reads the source at the checked commit (or a given one), by commit and never through the ref, and writes nothing. Per installed skill it reports unchanged, changed or unreadable, with a unified text diff against the live text, description and reference-file changes, scan warnings and whether an admin hand-edited it since import; installed skills whose folder left the source are flagged as removed and folders nothing installed uses are listed as added, each with the name conflicts and the scan block an install of it would meet. A skill whose diff passes a fixed size or work bound has no complete diff and its full text has to be read separately. The accept takes the commit and may name skills, each bound to the installed revision the admin saw; without named skills it is bound to the commit alone. It refuses unless the commit is still the source’s latest, refuses with SKILL_CHANGED and writes nothing if a named skill was edited since, never overwrites a hand-edited skill unless it is named, refuses a skill whose diff is incomplete (truncated or too large) unless it is named, and never updates a skill that no longer parses or whose folder left the source, naming it being refused as NOT_INSTALLABLE, and refuses scan warnings while the blocking setting is on. The accept transaction first takes the per-source lock that an install into the source also takes and re-reads the installed set; the accept compares the installed set it planned from with the set inside its transaction, so a skill installed into, or removed or detached from, the source since this accept read it refuses with SOURCE_CHANGED and the pin never moves past a skill this accept did not plan for. The same transaction cuts a new revision per updated skill, unverified and carrying the source commit, moves the pin only when nothing that changed upstream was left behind, and writes the audit entry; a latestSha that moved or a disable meanwhile rolls it all back. Runs already started keep the revisions they pinned. The CLI shows the diff, asks for confirmation (unless --yes) and, when skills are named with --skills, sends the installed revisions it showed. The dashboard’s Review update offers each changed skill for selection: one the scan blocks cannot be selected; one whose diff is incomplete or too large needs its full incoming text read at that commit and a confirmation that it was read; one hand-edited needs an explicit overwrite confirmation; those last two start unselected. A refusal meaning the reviewed state is stale (the source’s latest commit differs from the diffed one, an edited skill, an incomplete diff, a changed or disabled source, a source not yet checked) offers a Reload diff button rather than retrying.
features.title: Tracked skill-source updates: scheduled check, reviewed diff, bound accept

features.body: Track each pull request a workflow’s pull-request step or an Agent Run’s draft delivery opens, with its state, draft flag and title kept current from host webhooks, and list pull requests and tickets with per-row visibility.
features.detail: A PullRequest row, linked to the opening execution’s ledger row, records OPEN, MERGED or CLOSED (closed without merging), an isDraft flag, a title capped at 300 characters and opened, merged and closed times. Signed pull_request webhooks update only a row the platform already holds for that repository and number: closed, reopened, ready_for_review, converted_to_draft and edited (with a non-empty title) each update only that row. Close (only from OPEN) and reopen (only from CLOSED) are guarded by status, so a redelivery is a no-op; draft and title updates are not, so an out-of-order delivery can leave an older value. A pull request opened outside the platform is never created. An Agent Run with draft delivery inserts its row, on the run’s own ledger row, after the host accepts the draft. The row is only inserted, never updated, because an existing row with the same repository and number is a different pull request; the unique index refuses the collision. A failed write is logged and recorded on the run as a pr.record_failed event without failing it, since the branch is already pushed and the PR open. A workflow’s pull-request step links its own execution’s ledger row, or any ledger row of the same request when it has none. A re-push looks at the latest pull request on its own ledger row, whatever its status: an open one is updated, and a closed one fails the step before any other pull request is considered. When that one is merged, or there is none, the step adopts the newest open pull request of the same request and repository, and re-links it to the executing workflow’s own ledger row when that workflow has one, because CI webhooks signal the workflow a row names. The webhook lookups can match more than one connection row for a repository and take the newest. An id the platform generated names no tracker issue, so the tracker syncs for PR opened, workflow started, CI verdict, merge and run end are skipped for it, as is the knowledge-base page link write-back when a pull request opens, which also needs the flag to have been read and found false, so an unreadable flag skips it while the tracker sync is still attempted; the Slack merge note and merge evaluation row still run. Of the pull_request events only a merge signals the workflow (CI results arrive separately, through check_run webhooks). A merge is accepted from OPEN or CLOSED, so a reopen that was lost or late cannot strand it; a transient signal failure rolls the row back to its previous status, and a terminal one keeps MERGED. When the latest pull request on the executing workflow’s own ledger row (one it adopted included) was closed unmerged, the pull-request activity fails non-retryably with PR_CLOSED_BY_REVIEWER instead of opening a replacement or adopting another open one; a new run of the same request has its own ledger row and is not stopped. GET /api/v1/pull-requests (ENGINEER and above) lists newest first. A non-ADMIN sees a row only when the repository is reachable to them, and the ticket, request, cost and run on it come from its ledger row only while that row is on the same repository, the run only when the caller may see that run. GET /api/v1/tickets groups requests by external ticket id.
