A request counts for its requester, for anyone who can see one of its runs, and for anyone who reaches a repository it targets or holds a ledger row on; cost and pull-request aggregates count only repositories the caller reaches, so two teams can read one ticket differently. On the server, scope defaults to MINE (requests the caller submitted), pull requests to every state, and tickets exclude agent runs, channel tasks and requests whose ticket id the platform generated (an agent run, a channel task, a template launch that named no ticket, a PRD run, a scheduled work request, a PRD story the tracker gave no id) unless includeAutomated is set. The dashboard’s Pull requests page, by contrast, opens on OPEN.
features.title: Pull-request lifecycle & ticket views

features.body: Each agent runs on the platform’s Mastra tool loop or the Claude Code harness, and a run never switches an agent’s loop partway through.
features.detail: Resolution order: a caller-supplied pin (an eval side’s override), then the run’s own pin in WorkflowRun.agentRuntimes (an empty pin means the default, without reading the Agent), then the Agent version’s runtime (inherited along inheritsModelFrom, through the usual scope cascade and GLOBAL version pin), then the caller’s default. The implementer family and eval cases default to the run-pinned workspace.implementerRuntime setting; agent runs and generic agent nodes default to Mastra. A run, a channel-assistant turn included, snapshots every visible agent’s own runtime at start, resolved in the run’s scope under its version pins; an agent the snapshot lacks (one created later, or an agent run’s) is pinned at its first resolution with a compare-and-set, so parallel activities agree on whichever pinned first; code outside an activity, and an eval, which has no run, pin nothing. The run page shows what each agent ran on. Generic agent nodes resolve and pin their runtime the same way, defaulting to Mastra. Without a workspace they run on Mastra and trace agent.runtime_not_applicable when their agent is pinned to the harness; a node with workspace: true clones the run’s repository (the run’s branch once pushed, else the run’s base branch: payload.baseBranch when the launch named one, otherwise the repository’s default branch) and runs the pinned runtime there, harness included, committing and pushing nothing and destroying the checkout afterwards. A node’s @version ref does not choose its runtime: the pin is per agent key. Every runtime other than Mastra is served by a registered harness: a runtime value no harness serves fails non-retryably with HARNESS_UNAVAILABLE, and the implementer family, agent runs and checkout agent nodes select the harness and bind the agent’s model before building it (agent runs and checkout nodes before cloning).
features.title: Per-agent runtime, pinned per run

features.body: The worker decides every harness tool call, verifies the harness binary before each turn and treats an undecided call as a refusal.
features.detail: Each harness tool call is translated into a canonical vocabulary (read, search, write, shell) and decided in the worker by the same checks that guard the Mastra workspace tools: the shell-command scanner and audit line for shell, the sensitive-file block and pre-write content check for writes. File paths must be absolute; writes stay inside the checkout, reads and searches inside the checkout or the harness’s own .claude home directory, and search patterns may not be absolute or contain “..”. Tools the agent’s grant leaves out are left off the harness’s tool list and refused by the policy, as is any tool outside the six the harness maps, except the agent’s relayed MCP tools, which run in the worker. A harness is selectable only if it declares that the worker decides each of its tool calls; the registry refuses one that does not. A tool call the worker does not answer within the decision deadline, or whose decision throws, is refused, and writes to the harness’s own configuration (.claude/, CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, .mcp.json) are refused. Managed settings make the harness ignore the repository’s permission allow rules and disable bypass mode. Before every turn the container’s copy of the binary is compared by SHA-256 with the worker’s, re-copied on a mismatch, and a turn whose copy still differs fails with HARNESS_BINARY_UNVERIFIED.
features.title: Claude Code harness confinement

features.body: The three-persona review rejects only on what its reviewers said; a reviewer that cannot run is not a rejection of the code.
features.detail: Each persona’s output is schema-checked, and a CRITICAL verdict never approves. A budget, unpriced-model or missing-configuration failure in any persona fails the review activity, and all three failing throws a retryable REVIEW_NETWORK_UNAVAILABLE. When only some fail, the review stands and each missing persona is a critical REVIEWER_CRASH finding that asks for a human look. The summary a review-fix session starts from lists each finding’s reviewer, severity, description and suggested fix, and names a rejection that came with no findings.
features.title: Review failures are not verdicts

features.body: A repository’s team can attach rules that start a template when a signed GitHub delivery matches: a failed Actions run, or a label added to an issue.
features.detail: An Automation row holds the when (an event source and its filters), the what (a template and its options) and the limits (a cooldown, 30 minutes by default, and a daily cap, 10 runs by default). Two sources exist: github.workflow_run.failed (a completed, failed or timed-out run of a push, pull-request or scheduled workflow, from a branch of the repository itself, never a fork) and github.issues.labeled (a person labelling an open issue; bots, Apps and pull requests are ignored before any query). A signed webhook is normalized into an occurrence and handed to an engine that decides from the delivery alone, without calling the host (Temporal is asked only to confirm an in-flight run). It takes the first matching enabled automation (oldest repository row, then oldest automation), so one occurrence starts at most one run however many rows match. Before the limits, the source’s own ignore rule applies (the platform’s own work branches never react), the per-team or per-organization kill switch must be on (github.ciFailureTriggersEnabled is on by default, github.issueLabelAutomationsEnabled off), a source precondition holds (a pull-request failure needs an open pull request), a source that acts for a person finds one, the organization is within its monthly budget, and the automation’s template (its own, or the source’s built-in default) is active and one its source can start. The limits are then judged under a per-repository advisory lock across the repository’s whole ledger: not a commit the platform itself produced, not a subject (a commit, an issue) that already started a run, not inside the cooldown for its scope (a branch, an issue), no earlier run for that scope, started within the source’s lookback (36 hours for CI, 14 days for issue labels), still open (the ledger row is confirmed against Temporal, and a Temporal that cannot answer counts as running), and the automation’s rolling 24-hour cap. Each decision is one AutomationFire row: STARTED, a SUPPRESSED_* outcome or FAILED_TO_START. The workflow start is tried three times; if it never lands, the row becomes FAILED_TO_START and the delivery answers 503 so it can be sent again, and a redelivery or a manager’s retry takes a FAILED_TO_START decision again. A manager can retry any decision that started no run; every limit applies again and the earlier row stays, marked retried. One builder makes a run’s options at save time and at fire time and checks them against the template’s input schema. Saving an enabled automation, or enabling one, is a launch decision for the saver; managing needs ADMIN, or a LEAD or ADMIN member of the owning team, and reading needs repository membership, a shared team included, and, under an enforcing access gate, a current host permission.
features.title: Event automations start runs from GitHub events

features.body: A failed GitHub Actions run is diagnosed from its logs; in fix mode a code-fixable failure gets a draft pull request into the branch that failed.
features.detail: ci-triage-and-fix is library content: an ordinary spec the interpreter runs, started by a CI-failure automation or by hand with a run id. Its first step, triageCiFailure, takes the run by id, never a URL, and reads the run, its failed jobs and their logs from the run’s own repository. It ends SKIPPED, posting nothing, when the run belongs to another repository, did not fail, was triggered by something other than a push, pull request or schedule, comes from a fork commit, is for a branch other than the payload’s, is a tag or a deleted branch, or is a pull-request failure whose pull request is no longer open from that branch. Log text is redacted for common token shapes, screened with the INJECTION patterns (every character of the tail given to the triager, about 40,000 characters shared across the failed jobs), and given to the ciTriager agent (no tools, model inherited from the planner), which returns a typed verdict. Code, not the model, decides fix or report, so the model can veto a fix but cannot start one the rules refuse. Code reports instead of fixing when the mode is not fix (the default mode is triage, diagnose only), no log could be read, the logs look like injection or the screen did not complete, a pull request’s head has moved since the failure, the category is not regression, test_bug, configuration or dependency (flaky, infrastructure and unknown are never fixed, and a trigger can only narrow that set), or confidence is below the trigger’s floor (0.6 by default, between 0.3 and 1). On the fix path the implementer receives the diagnosis fenced as untrusted data, and a change touching .github/workflows or .github/actions, or adding a symlink or a submodule, is refused before anything is pushed. Lint, typecheck and tests follow, then verifyCiFix labels the fix, then a draft pull request opens into the failing branch. Its CI is waited on by signal or poll and the fix is revised while that CI fails, up to maxCiFixAttempts times (2 by default, at most 5), with the draft’s own CI logs redacted, screened whole and fenced; a first attempt that changes no file ends the run as a report, and a revision that changed nothing counts as a spent attempt instead of waiting out CI. For a failure on a pull request the platform posts or updates one marked comment (unless the trigger turns commentOnPullRequest off), rendered from structured fields with model text neutralized (no markdown structure, links or mentions). Nothing is merged, and the template has no approval node.
features.title: CI failure triage and draft fix

features.body: For a failing pull request, a trigger may ask that the fix land as a commit on the author’s branch instead of a draft; a setting that is off by default and several refusals stand between the request and the push.
features.detail: pullRequestDelivery: push is a request, not a grant. An automation cannot save it unless the built-in template is its template and github.ciFixPushToPullRequestEnabled is on for its team (default off). pushCiFixToPullRequest then pushes only if all of these hold at the moment of the push: this execution is the one a CI-failure automation started (its ledger row names this request and workflow id, so a re-run or a hand-started run never qualifies, and a run with a launching user is refused); the run’s template is the built-in one and the automation, not the payload, asks for push; the setting is on; the failure is a pull-request run whose pull request is still open from this repository with the failing branch as its head; the branch is not the default, not protected and not matched by github.ciFixNeverPushBranches (main, master, develop, trunk, release/**, releases/** and hotfix/** by default); the commit is on the run’s own work branch and is a fast-forward of the branch tip; and it touches no workflow file. Anything else returns pushed: false with a reason and the template opens the draft instead. The ref moves with force: false. The commit is recorded on the ledger row before the push, so its later CI failure is suppressed as the platform’s own output (SUPPRESSED_OWN_OUTPUT) even if the activity dies right after pushing. The run then polls the pull request’s CI on the pushed commit; on failure it makes at most one follow-up (none when the trigger allows no revisions, whatever maxCiFixAttempts is above 1), then reports and leaves the pull request to a person. The work branch is deleted afterwards unless a follow-up could not be pushed.
features.title: A CI fix can be pushed onto a pull request’s own branch

features.body: The command the triager says reproduces the failure is run on the failing branch and on the fix; the result labels the fix and never blocks it.
features.detail: The command is model output read from untrusted logs. It runs only if it is the whole run: of a step the host reports as failed in a failed job, read from the workflow file in the workspace, contains no ${{ }} expression, is at most 1,000 characters (a longer one is dropped, never cut) and is cleared by the shell command scanner. The fix branch is fetched before the command runs, so no credential is used after the branch’s code has run. The command runs on the failing branch, the tree is reset and cleaned, and it runs again on the fix, each with an 8-minute limit; both outputs are stored as an artifact. The status is verified, not_reproduced, still_failing or unverified, shown as a Verified or Unverified line in the pull request and the run result. Nothing is installed first, so a command that needs the workflow’s setup steps fails both times; that is reported, not read as proof the fix is wrong. The step is a warning-on-failure node, and delivery proceeds whatever the status.
features.title: A CI fix is reproduced before and after, but only labelled

features.body: A launch may name payload.baseBranch; the checkout, the diff and the pull request target follow it.
features.detail: The gateway validates it on template launches, template webhook calls and retries (agent runs refuse a work branch with the same error, while an invalid name fails request validation): it must be a valid git branch name and must not be one of the platform’s own work branches, otherwise 400 INVALID_BASE_BRANCH. The work-branch rule is decided once, at launch, so changing the branch prefix mid-run cannot fail a run part-way. The worker re-checks the name in every activity that clones for a run (BASE_BRANCH_REFUSED, non-retryable), because the clone is single-branch and every activity must agree on which branch it holds. The payload is the one place a base is recorded, so a retry or re-run of a fix for release/1.4 is still a fix for it. CodeResult.baseBranch carries it into fix sessions and makes the pull-request step open into the branch the change was cut from. A CI-failure automation sets it to the failing branch.
features.title: A run can be based on a branch other than the default

features.body: One row-based coverage model decides whether every agent and the embedding model can reach a credential; the same model refuses a credential delete that would strand one and fails the credentials item of setup readiness on gaps in the agent set the worker’s boot gate resolves, plus a missing apiBase on a custom provider, which boot does not check (the embeddings item fails on any embedding gap).
features.detail: credentialGaps derives, from rows alone and without decrypting any key, which agents and the embedding model have no credential they can call. An agent’s model comes from its own spec or its inheritsModelFrom chain. A pinned credential counts when it exists, is for that provider and is reachable from the agent’s scope; otherwise the TEAM, ORGANIZATION, GLOBAL cascade picks the first reachable credential, as the worker does, and an unusable pin falls back to the cascade. A provider that is not built in also needs an apiBase on it. A channel or workflow-template agent runs for whichever team owns the run, so any credential for its provider counts. The embedding model follows the worker’s own rules, including that a pin to a credential of another provider is used as-is and is therefore a gap of its own. Deleting a credential answers 409 CREDENTIAL_IN_USE with the dependents unless force=true; a forced delete records what it left uncovered in the audit entry, and a team admin is refused, and shown dependents, only for its own team’s agents. GET /credentials adds usage.leavesWithoutCredential for the same question, and the dashboard’s delete confirmation lists it and then sends the forced delete. The admin-only readiness route reports four items (credentials, embeddings, GitHub access, a real repository connection) and computes the agent set the worker’s boot check resolves from the same shared code: the steps of every installed template’s active and experiment versions, plus channelAssistant when a Slack channel exists. The credentials item fails only on a gap in that set or a required key with no platform-wide agent; every other gap, at any scope, is returned in gaps with a blocking flag. The same route lists each provider with the GLOBAL agents that call it and whether any of them lacks a usable credential. The embedding model is counted toward its provider only when the provider is what is missing: no credential at all, or a custom provider with no apiBase on an embedding that pins no credential. A spec the platform cannot embed with, no embedding config, or a credential pinned to another provider (or pinned and lacking an apiBase) is reported on the embeddings item and does not mark the provider as uncovered. The worker, for its part, refuses to start until assertConfigReady has resolved each of those GLOBAL agents for real (decrypting its key) and checked the embedding model’s rows only.
features.title: Credential coverage, delete guard and setup readiness

features.body: An agent’s pinned credential is used for its model call only if it exists, matches the model’s provider and is in the run’s scope; otherwise the provider cascade runs.
features.detail: The resolver uses the agent’s own pin or, if it has none, the pin on the row its model was inherited from; one unusable pin goes straight to the cascade. A pin is accepted only when the row exists, its provider (trimmed, lowercased) equals the provider the spec routes to, and its scope is GLOBAL, the run’s organization or the run’s team. A miss logs that the pin is not usable and falls back to the provider-name cascade (TEAM, ORGANIZATION, GLOBAL), so a stale pin cannot send one vendor’s key to another vendor’s API. The gateway checks reachability when an agent is created, edited or restored, and the client cache is keyed on a SHA-256 digest of the whole key and bounded with least-recently-used eviction.
features.title: A credential pin is honoured only where the run could reach it

features.body: Chat, embedding and Claude Code proxy calls resolve the provider host, connect only to a checked address and refuse redirects.
features.detail: modelCallFetch wraps the list guard: each connection is resolved, every answer checked and the socket pinned to a checked address, with redirects refused because a model call carries the prompt and the API key. Every built-in client (anthropic, openai, google) and every OpenAI-compatible client is constructed with it whether or not the credential sets an apiBase, as are the embedding clients and the Claude Code model proxy’s upstream fetch. A host that is, or resolves to, a private address is reachable only if it is listed in models.privateNetworkHosts; loopback, link-local, cloud-metadata, unspecified, multicast and reserved addresses stay refused whatever is listed. Saving a credential checks its apiBase as text only; the resolve-and-pin happens at the test, discovery, refresh and call. The list is read on every request behind the settings cache and an unreadable setting degrades to empty, so an unlisted in-cluster model server fails before any request is sent. This closes the gap between the text check at credential save and the call: a name that later resolves, or redirects, to an internal host no longer receives the prompt and the key.
features.title: Worker-built model, embedding and proxy calls go through the outbound guard

features.body: Agents may sit on different providers at once; adapters make structured output, proxied OpenAI and embeddings behave across them.
features.detail: OpenAI-compatible providers (OpenRouter, Ollama, vLLM and others) are wrapped by schemaInPromptMiddleware: the adapter sends plain json_object mode and drops the response schema, so for a structured call the middleware appends the JSON schema and a return-only-the-JSON instruction to the system prompt, while built-in providers, which enforce schemas natively, are untouched. An openai credential with an apiBase uses Chat Completions (most proxies serve nothing else); without one it uses the Responses API. Agent saves and the embedding config require <provider>/<model-id> and store the provider lowercased, so pricing, the catalog and the harness check read one canonical form. Embeddings accept openai, google and OpenAI-compatible endpoints, requested 1536 wide (except at an OpenAI-compatible endpoint that refused the parameter); on a 400 from an OpenAI-compatible endpoint the call is retried once without the dimensions parameter and the endpoint remembered as refusing it, so only a model natively 1536 wide still works there (an openai or google 400 is not retried). Anthropic is refused as an embedding provider. A model that cannot be built (a non-built-in provider with no apiBase) throws a non-retryable MODEL_CONFIG_INVALID.
features.title: Providers side by side: structured output, OpenAI endpoints and embeddings

features.body: Agent repository workspaces start with the resolvers in WORKSPACE_DNS, public by default.
features.detail: createWorkspace adds one --dns flag per entry, each shell-quoted, to docker run. The list is read from the worker’s environment (comma-separated IPs): unset or empty gives 1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8, and an invalid list falls back to that default with one logged warning. At worker boot the environment check stops the worker on an entry that is not an IP, is zoned IPv6, is loopback or unspecified, or, while WORKSPACE_BLOCK_METADATA is on, is one of the metadata addresses the workspace blackholes. It exists for split-horizon repository hosts whose public answer is unreachable from the cluster. Like the other workspace infrastructure settings it is environment-only: not a registry setting and not an admin form. Only repository workspaces made by createWorkspace are described here.
features.title: Workspace containers get a configurable list of DNS resolvers

features.body: Dashboard pages explain the product inline: help tips, page-header links, a lifecycle overview, a first-run checklist, an optional tour, node help and a run verdict, with a built-in docs reader and text search.
features.detail: A help tip is a small button that opens a popover on hover, focus or click, showing either a glossary definition or the text its caller wrote, plus a link to the matching doc. The glossary and the table of doc links are constants compiled into the web app: opening a tip reads that local table and a doc link only builds an in-app URL, so neither calls the gateway or reads platform data (the link is a Next.js Link, which may prefetch the static doc page from the web server). A doc link is an ordinary in-app route into a docs reader, which serves only the top level of the repository’s docs directory; its pages are generated statically, so they show the docs as they were when the web app was built. The reader’s index also searches the doc text: once typing pauses, the browser asks a route of the web server (behind the web proxy’s sign-in redirect, which checks only that a session cookie is present, as for the docs pages themselves; the query is cut to a bounded length) for the best matching sections, which return as highlight segments rather than HTML, so only those few results are downloaded. The server builds the index once per process from the same files, begins it at start-up without delaying start-up, and does not keep a failed build; if the request fails, title and summary matching still works and the next edit retries. The Home page opens the overview by default when, on the first load (Mine scope unless already switched), the attention, active and succeeded request lists are all empty; switching scope does not re-decide it. Start work renders it collapsed; the node palette and governance pages carry tips of the same kind, and some forms carry static help text and doc links. The OAuth consent screen opens its docs link in a new tab so the reader does not navigate away from the grant. Home also shows people who are not admins a first-run checklist whose steps tick from data the person can already read (a visible repository, a request of theirs, a gate they answered, a merged pull request from their request), and shows admins a governance guide once the setup readiness check passes; each can be dismissed, and the dismissal is kept in that browser’s local storage only. A Take the tour button starts a short role-dependent tour that points at the sidebar and its links (one step points at nothing and is centred); it never starts by itself and is recorded as seen when it ends, in the same browser storage. In the workflow editor, selecting a node shows its type’s help. Each run page opens with a verdict banner derived from the run record and the run’s visible open gates, with a collapsed guide to reading the page: it names a cause only for an error the dashboard classifies, otherwise says none is stated, and it cannot say who a gate waits on. Start work offers a chooser between modes and a sample-task button that only fills fields and never launches.
features.title: In-app guided help

limits.body: HubSpot and generic HTTP API lack concrete genericActions handlers.
limits.detail: readSource/writeOutcome/runTool return ok:true with placeholder:true for several types. Notion, Zendesk, tracker and Slack have specific real handlers; MCP is executed separately.
limits.title: Some integration labels are placeholders

limits.body: A failed post-diff security gate can leave code on a remote branch.
limits.detail: executeImplementation commits/pushes first, then scans the diff and may throw SECURITY_GATE_FAILURE. Exhausted TDD iterations can also return failing tests. Do not interpret activity failure as “nothing was published.” Agent Run delivery uses a different trusted-container path.
limits.title: Engineering push happens before the critical diff gate

limits.body: The approval guard lives in writeOutcome, conditional on a recorded publish decision.
limits.detail: A run with no recorded decision is not gated by assertApprovalSatisfied. runTool, MCP and arbitrary shell paths are not covered by that helper. Template design and tool permissions remain important.
limits.title: Outcome policy is not a universal outbound-write guard

limits.body: The external call completes before the outcome-reference row is inserted.
limits.detail: A crash between remote success and local persistence can repeat a write. Concurrent invocations may race the read-before-write check. The ledger reduces duplicates but is not a transactional outbox with remote idempotency guarantees.
limits.title: Write retry ledger is best-effort, not exactly-once

limits.body: The run-start pin applies to GLOBAL lineage, not every scope.
limits.detail: fetchActiveAgent looks up active template/channel/team/org versions before applying the GLOBAL version clause. An explicit key@version is threaded through the same map, so it does not force a matching version at a more-specific scope. The runtime is the exception: the run pins it at start even when a scoped row supplied it.
limits.title: Scoped agent versions remain live

limits.body: Opt-in egress uses bridge networking, unreachable DNS and add-host entries.
limits.detail: Direct-IP traffic is not blocked by this allowlist; wildcard entries are skipped. The resolvers an agent repository workspace is given come from WORKSPACE_DNS, a deployer’s choice and not a boundary: pointing them at an internal resolver lets code in the workspace resolve every name that resolver knows. Docker shares the host kernel, and the worker holds the daemon socket. Treat that host as a privileged trust boundary.
limits.title: DNS egress filtering is not a network firewall

limits.body: Soft scores do not automatically stop a run, and aggregate score is not the authoritative gate result.
limits.detail: decideGate blocks hard floors. judgeAdvisory:false can enable a judge threshold. The workflow still chooses which eval nodes to include and how to branch on their outputs.
limits.title: Judge scores are advisory by default

limits.body: Flake rate and judge/human kappa have configurable ceilings but nothing stores them, so only the quarantined share of golden cases is shown, as it is now.
limits.detail: The suite-health endpoint counts each dataset’s quarantined and flake-screened cases and returns the configured thresholds beside them, so its stale rate has no history. A trend filtered to a template keeps results of runs of that template, so offline harness rows, which have no run, drop out.
limits.title: Suite health stores only the stale rate

limits.body: A staging or monitoring signal reports work done elsewhere.
limits.detail: The graph waits and branches on flags, returning FAILED or TIMED_OUT when necessary. A rollback-required termination is not an actual rollback command.
limits.title: Release-gate templates do not perform deployments

limits.body: A Mastra Agent Run debits per step and every harness turn per model call; Mastra implementer turns and ordinary multi-step generate loops debit at completion.
limits.detail: A model call can overshoot a checked budget before returning, and a harness turn re-checks the budget only after each call, so an exhausted budget stops it one call late. Through the worker’s model proxy every call, side calls included, is debited as its response ends, and a call cut off mid-stream is charged the input and output the provider had reported. Without the proxy a call is debited only once the next begins, calls the harness makes without streaming a message are charged when the turn ends and never trigger the check, and a turn stopped by its deadline, or whose process dies, is metered from its streamed messages, which miss those calls; a turn that ends at its turn cap is metered from the harness’s own totals. A harness turn that fails while its activity is cancelled reports the cancellation, and what that turn spent is not accrued. Workflows with no run have no ActiveWorkflow ledger; a per-execution token cap summed from their trace rows and this worker’s unpersisted calls bounds them instead. It cannot see calls still in flight on another worker, and a failed budget read lets the call through.
limits.title: Budget precision differs by execution path

limits.body: Launches and each later model call are refused once cached spend has reached the cap, so spend can still land after it is crossed, and some spend is outside it.
limits.detail: The guard runs before each budgeted model call and refuses only when the cached organization spend has already reached the cap. Up to one cache window of new calls from every run of the organization at once, plus the full cost of every call or harness turn already admitted, can land after the cap is crossed: an admitted call completes and bills in full, its cost accrues to the ledger only after it returns, and a Claude Code harness call accrues only once it ends. Concurrent launches see the same total. A spend or cap read that fails lets the call through. Spend with no derivable organization is outside the cap, and a repo-less channel task bills its channel, so the organization cap never refuses it. An epic’s planning is attributed to the first repository it names even when the epic spans organizations; each child is billed to its own repository’s. An unpriced model is refused when the run’s billed organization (the same billedOrgId rule as the cap, so a PRD run or a code-route channel task counts through its connection) has a cap, or when a runless workflow’s spend owner does, and under a channel cap; a repo-less channel task bills its channel, so it is not refused on the organization’s account.
limits.title: The organization USD cap is checked before each call, so spend can overshoot it

limits.body: A run whose workflow ended without finalizing still counts as in flight until a sweep reaches it, and only while the sweep is enabled.
limits.detail: A run is looked up only after a ten-minute grace, and a sweep asks about a bounded batch, never-checked runs first, so a crowd of live runs cannot hold the batch. A failed Temporal lookup leaves the run alone, because a live run must never be billed. The schedule is set from the environment when the gateway starts and is paused when disabled, after which stranded runs count against the cap indefinitely. A run that closed long ago is ended silently, with no Slack notice, channel report or tracker update, so a first sweep over history does not post for old orphans. Reaped spend is billed to the month of finalization, so a run reaped late lands in the month it is reaped. A dashboard cancel of a run whose execution is gone leaves the run for the reaper to bill rather than ending it unbilled.
limits.title: The run reaper bounds unfinalized spend; it does not remove the window

limits.body: Team and organization breakdowns read the owner stamped on each trace row.
limits.detail: Rows older than the owner columns, spend with no derivable owner and rows written while the run lookup failed land under no team. There is no per-repository breakdown, and the platform-wide report is ADMIN-only.
limits.title: Usage is attributed when a trace is written

limits.body: A run’s workflow span appears only when its workflow code ends, an externally terminated run never exports one, and a signal is a link rather than a parent.
limits.detail: Each run has a workflow span, exported from a Temporal sink when its workflow code ends, so a long run (an approval wait included) has no span in a trace backend until it finishes and its activities sit under a parent the backend does not yet have. A run terminated or timed out from outside never runs workflow code, so no span is exported and its activities stay under a missing parent. A plain error thrown from workflow code fails the workflow task, which is retried, so it exports nothing until the run ends; RunnableWorkflow turns its own graph failures into a failed run, so those export a failed span. A final workflow task that Temporal rejects or retries exports the span again, with the same span id. A run cancelled while awaiting an activity is recorded as cancelled, not as an error. The span covers the run, not the idle time between activities. A signal or update context reaches only activities scheduled after it, and only the newest one is linked; work already running and earlier signals are not. The worker’s own signals are not stamped. Worker and gateway structured logs export over OTLP, and audit lines do only inside an activity; other plain console output stays on stdout. A tool call that fails input validation or names no tool never executes, so it is recorded from the step results with zero duration, and only when generation returned: if it throws, those calls are lost. HTTP instrumentation requires the --import preload, and the start scripts and Dockerfile commands silence one Node deprecation code only (DEP0205, the module register hook the OpenTelemetry loader still uses).
limits.title: Tracing and log export have deliberate gaps

limits.body: With the claude-code runtime and no model proxy, the harness receives the model key inside the container the agent controls; through the proxy it holds a token good only for its own turn’s model calls.
limits.detail: The key, or the proxy’s turn token, stays off command lines and every tool call passes the worker-side policy, but what the agent runs in that container can read it. The token spends only on the Messages API, against the run’s budget, at the credential’s own host, until the turn ends. The proxy’s upstream calls to that host are resolved, checked and pinned like other model calls; only the no-proxy path, where the container reaches the host directly, is outside that check (under an environment proxy the upstream call is checked but not pinned). The shipped compose files run the proxy (HARNESS_MODEL_PROXY_PORT); a deployment that sets no port hands the harness the key. This applies to implementer-family sessions and to agent runs whose agent selects the harness; an agent run’s diff is still judged and published from a fresh container. The repository’s own CLAUDE.md, .claude settings and hooks load, but managed settings make the harness ignore the repository’s permission allow rules, so a tool call the policy does not approve is refused, and writes to .claude/, CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md and .mcp.json are refused. Only anthropic/<model> specs are supported; any other fails non-retryably with HARNESS_UNSUPPORTED_MODEL. A credential base URL can route through a gateway.
limits.title: Without the model proxy, the Claude Code runtime puts a model key in the workspace

limits.body: An Idempotency-Key binds permanently to its first ticket, repository, description and budget tier.
limits.detail: Ledger rows are written before the Temporal start, so a same-key request during the start gets 409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_IN_PROGRESS. A failed stamp after a successful start, or failed compensation after a failed start, leaves the key in progress until an operator repairs the rows. Keys are never swept, and only POST /work-requests honours them.
limits.title: Work-request idempotency keys never expire

limits.body: This explorer is a source snapshot, not an operational test or security audit.
limits.detail: Routes, schemas, seed specs and tests establish implemented surfaces. No infrastructure, external credentials, LLM calls or full platform test suite were exercised for this analysis. Test presence is not a passing test result.
limits.title: Implementation is not live deployment proof

limits.body: Discovery lists ids from the keys the platform holds; it supplies no prices and judges retirement by what one key can see.
limits.detail: Discovery reads no price from a listing, so an admin still enters every number that feeds USD budgets. Only GLOBAL credentials are asked, so a model reachable through a team or organization key is not found. Listings follow a bounded number of pages and drop non-text models by a name filter; a listing past the cap, empty, or with a continuation it cannot follow is incomplete: it still records new suggestions but deletes nothing and flags no retirement candidates. A retirement flag is a hint measured against one key’s view, and an apiBase on a private address is refused as blocked address unless its host is listed in models.privateNetworkHosts. The list is matched against the apiBase host text. The fetch still resolves the name and connects only to an address it checked, but nothing verifies that a listed name points at the intended server, so a listed name may reach any private-range address it resolves to; loopback, link-local and metadata answers stay refused. A built-in provider behind an apiBase never yields retirement candidates, because its listing is the proxy’s, not the vendor’s. The list applies to every provider credential, and to run-time model and embedding calls too, not to one credential. The schedule’s cron and enabled flag take effect only after a gateway restart.
limits.title: Model discovery finds ids, not prices

limits.body: Connected means the first connection was made, not that Temporal is reachable now, and while it is pending workflow operations are refused.
limits.detail: The health body reports connecting until the first connection succeeds and connected afterwards; after that the SDK’s channel reconnects on its own and the gateway does not probe, so connected does not mean reachable at this moment. While the state is connecting no workflow start, signal, cancel or schedule operation can run, and nothing queues them: the caller gets a retryable refusal (usually 503). Per-channel and per-work-request schedules are not re-synchronized when the connection comes up, so a schedule that diverged while Temporal was down is corrected only by the next write to its row; the environment-driven system schedules are corrected at the next gateway start. Only the scheduled-work list reports an unknown state (exists: null, unavailable: true) instead of a missing schedule; other reads that need Temporal, including the status of the system schedule settings, answer 503. The shipped app Compose file still starts the gateway only after Temporal reports healthy, so the background connection protects other deployments and later outages, not a Compose start.
limits.title: Temporal health is the first connection, not live reachability

limits.body: The refresh agent reads untrusted pricing pages; the guards confine where it can write, not whether it can be wrong.
limits.detail: The workspace has network access and a shell. The path guard and checkScope keep the diff to the catalog file, the prompt treats fetched text as data, and a failed provider listing reaches the agent only as fixed words, but a hostile or misread page can still put a wrong price inside that file. The runTests gate runs in warn mode, so a failing test is recorded and the run continues to a draft PR; CI on the draft is the hard check. A run that stops because the previous refresh is still open ends SUCCESS, so a stuck schedule looks green, and the guard trusts the git binary in the container.
limits.title: The catalog refresh contains untrusted input, not prevents it

limits.body: The pull request exists, ready for review, before any person has signed off; in consensus-review it also precedes every reviewer agent (four-eyes runs its agent review loop first).
limits.detail: four-eyes and consensus-review open a non-draft pull request and run CI before their gate, so opening it can notify Slack, sync trackers and request CODEOWNERS reviewers early, and a run that ends FAILED or TIMED_OUT leaves it open. Of the built-in templates only model-catalog-refresh and ci-triage-and-fix request a draft pull request, and there is no step that marks a draft ready. Only these two templates and ci-triage-and-fix guard a no-op CI fix with retryIfUnchanged; the other repush templates can still wait out a CI signal that never comes.
limits.title: Gated templates open a ready PR before the gate

limits.body: A host has at most one PAT and at most one App, and a repository on a host with neither is reachable only with a user’s own token.
limits.detail: A repository on another host with no recorded credentials fails with REPO_CREDENTIAL_HOST_MISMATCH unless its launcher saved their own token; two Apps or per-organization PATs on one host are not expressible. A login records the account it was read from, and the takeover check verifies against that account. Only a login with no recorded source (written before it was recorded) held by a user with several linked GitHub accounts is unverifiable, so no takeover is detected for it until a sign-in records one; a non-github.com host with no credential gets none either (a github.com account with no applicable credential is asked unauthenticated, so the check is rate-limited). Installations are registered only by an admin: GitHub’s events can retire, reactivate or rename a registered one, never add one.
limits.title: Host credentials are one set per host

limits.body: Skill pinning covers runs that have a WorkflowRun row, and it is not a freeze of every skill input.
limits.detail: The channel assistant’s own conversational runs pin GLOBAL agent versions and skill revisions on the row they create, for the turn’s team and organization (taken from its Slack channel when the turn does not name them), and the run-pinned settings at the scope the turn reads them with: its template, its channel and that tenant. An epic’s children are runs of their own and pin at their own start. A skill with no entry in the map, such as one created after the run began, resolves its current revision. isActive is read live, within the config cache window. A missing pinned revision row falls back to the live text, with a warning in the log and, inside an activity, a skill.pinned_revision_missing trace event, which is the swap pinning exists to prevent. A repo-less channel task finds its tenant by Slack channel id, which is unique only per workspace.
limits.title: Skill revision pins have gaps

limits.body: Grouping attempts by request reads every matching execution identity before status filtering and paging.
limits.detail: The cost therefore grows with history. A request appears once its first execution row is recorded. A retry amends only the attempt description (and the payload description when one exists), so a custom workflow that reads another input field does not see the added instructions.
limits.title: The request list groups before it paginates

limits.body: Pinning to a commit fixes what is read; it does not vouch for the author, the files kept beside the text, or the host.
limits.detail: Reference files are stored unscanned, so whatever first reads them to an agent or a person must scan them first. The host check reads address text and literal addresses, and a fetch resolves and pins the host it connects to, so a listed name is trusted to mean the intended server only as far as that resolution allows. Commit signatures are not checked. The scheduled check asks about the ref, not the history of the source’s path, so any commit on the ref flags the source, and in a monorepo an unrelated commit reads as an update whose diff shows nothing. A diff and an accept each read the whole new commit through the bounded fetch, so reviewing then accepting costs two budgeted fetches beside the check’s one request. An accept updates only skills already installed: a skill added upstream is listed, and can be installed only once an accept has moved the pin (an install reads the pinned commit), one removed upstream is flagged and stays, and an upstream rename is shown and not applied. Reference files from an accept are stored unscanned, like an import’s. There is no way to decline a change, so a skill left behind keeps the source flagged. An install into a source reads only the pinned commit and an accept moves the pin only when nothing changed upstream is left behind, so a hand-edited or unparseable skill that is never accepted keeps the source flagged and keeps skills added upstream uninstallable. Hand-edit detection compares content with the last revision an import or accept cut, so a revert to the same content reads as unedited. The review is an ADMIN flow in the dashboard, the API and the CLI. Each full-text read the dashboard makes costs one more budgeted fetch of the whole source. Only imports (a first import or an install into an existing source) take the name-allocation lock, so the skill API can still create a name an import has just checked.
limits.title: Skill import is pinned and bounded, not verified

limits.body: The guard checks URL text early and resolves and pins at connection time, but its opt-in is per connector rather than per address.
limits.detail: The text check alone does not resolve a name, so the dispatcher resolves it at connection time, refuses the request if any answer is internal and connects only to a checked address; a name that cannot be resolved is refused. The opt-in applies to the connector as a whole, so with it on every other private address is reachable from that connector, not just the one service the admin meant. The save-time check covers the stored configuration only; environment-variable fallbacks are checked when a guarded connector runs or Jira field detection is called, so a refused one surfaces at that point. A base URL that points at loopback is refused with or without the opt-in. GitHub Issues follows a redirect to another origin only if that origin passes the strict guard, so a private-network server that redirects to a different private origin is refused. The hop cap and the header allowlist are fixed in code. An MCP connection’s opt-in is per connection and applies only to that connection’s own origin: with it on, its URL may name or resolve to a private-range address, while redirects to other origins stay strict. Where the pin itself stops is in the resolve-and-pin coverage card.
limits.title: The connector SSRF guard resolves and pins, and the opt-in is coarse

limits.body: The pin covers the call sites that use the guarded fetch; a proxy, a Claude Code harness run without the model proxy, and the GitHub API clients sit outside it.
limits.detail: With a process-wide environment proxy (NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY, or --use-env-proxy on the command line or in NODE_OPTIONS) the host is resolved and checked locally first, but the proxy resolves it again, so the connection is not pinned to the checked answer; a network that resolves names only through its proxy fails closed. The worker’s chat and embedding clients and the Claude Code model proxy’s upstream calls take the same guard (modelCallFetch), so a public apiBase name that resolves to a private address is refused on an agent’s model call as well as on the credential test. A Claude Code harness run without the model proxy calls the credential’s host from inside the workspace container, outside the worker and outside that guard. Octokit and GitHub Enterprise API calls, the GitHub connection test against the saved API URL (a GitHub Enterprise host is often private), the sign-in organization-membership check that auto-approves a GitHub sign-up (it sends the platform credential to the instance’s API URL and follows no redirect), and the sign-in library’s Okta discovery fetch use a plain fetch; fixed public hosts such as Slack, Linear, Notion and Figma are not pinned either. For a repository on a GitHub Enterprise host every hop of the CI-log download may reach a private address, so a redirect from that host can aim the worker at another internal service (without the token). 198.18.0.0/15 is treated as private, so behind a fake-IP proxy tool every connector needs its opt-in, and provider probes, model discovery, the catalog refresh and the model and embedding calls need the host listed in models.privateNetworkHosts, and bundle URLs, which have no opt-in, are refused. The bare-fetch invariant is a text tripwire over a fixed module list and does not see an aliased fetch or another HTTP client.
limits.title: Resolve-and-pin covers listed call sites, not every outbound request

limits.body: A team marked inactive keeps its members’ repository access and its shares.
limits.detail: Team membership predicates read membership rows only. Removing a repository share is what ends a shared team’s access.
limits.title: Deactivating a team does not remove repository access

limits.body: A pull-request webhook updates a row; of those events only a merge reaches the workflow, and only a delivered webhook updates anything.
limits.detail: Only pull requests that a workflow’s pull-request step or an Agent Run’s draft delivery opens get a row. CLOSED and MERGED come only from signed pull_request webhooks, so without delivery (polling-only CI, a lost delivery) the row stays OPEN, and the list and the PR_CLOSED_BY_REVIEWER refusal both depend on delivery. An Agent Run’s own execution has ended by the time its pull request merges, so a merge is recorded without a signal, and its generated ticket id is never synced to the tracker. If an older row still holds the pull request’s number in that repository, the new row is not written. A run waiting on its merge keeps waiting after its pull request is closed unmerged, until a merge arrives or the wait ends; the refusal appears only when a later push step reaches the pull-request activity. A webhook for a pull request the platform did not open finds no row and changes nothing. Reopening restores only CLOSED to OPEN, and event times come from the host’s payload when it parses, else the time of receipt. The ticket list shows the tracker’s title, status and link as captured when a request was submitted, from the newest visible request that holds an answer; they are not refreshed. RunInput.ticketIsSynthetic marks an id the platform generated: the template launch and template webhook fallbacks, PRD runs (PRD-… ids), scheduled work requests (…-SCHED-… ids), event-automation runs (ci-<run>-<attempt> for a failed Actions run, issue-<number>-<hash> for a labelled issue) and PRD stories the tracker gave no id; it defaults to false, so a user- or tracker-supplied id is never flagged. Agent runs and channel tasks are flagged and also recognised by template origin, template name or channel id; the channel assistant files no request of its own. An adopted pull request is re-linked only when the executing workflow has a ledger row of its own; without one it stays linked to its earlier execution, whose workflow receives the CI signal, and the close check does not cover it. Adoption matches by request and repository only and no head branch is stored, so after a branch prefix change or a missed close webhook the adopted pull request can have a different head branch than the one pushed. A retry is refused while a live ledger row of its request exists, a scheduled fire’s or a template-launched run’s included, and a fire is skipped while a live non-fire row does; each row is confirmed with Temporal before it blocks (the allocator’s own conflict row included), and each check reads the ledger and then acts, so a retry and a fire that both read before either writes its row can still push the same branch, and the later one to reach the pull-request step adopts and re-links the other’s pull request, so the other waits for a CI signal that now goes to the adopter until its wait ends.
limits.title: Pull-request tracking records the host’s state; it does not steer the run

limits.body: A modal has no private reply channel, so some Slack confirmations are public in the thread.
limits.detail: An approve or reject button always opens the modal, so every approval is answered by a modal submission, which carries no response_url. The note that a multi-approver step still needs approvals is therefore always posted publicly in the announcement’s thread, the thread known only from the click that opened the modal, where a one-click answer would have got a private reply. A failed post is dropped silently and not retried; the decision itself is already recorded. The message edit that shows the decision applies only to the message the worker recorded.
limits.title: Slack modal approvals confirm in the thread, not privately

limits.body: Agents a run’s start snapshot lacks are pinned at first use, so an edit made before then reaches the run.
limits.detail: An agent created after the run started, and an agent run’s agent (resolved in a narrower scope than the run’s), are pinned where first resolved; an agent whose inheritsModelFrom chain was broken at start is left out of the snapshot and fails where it is used. The save-time model check follows the platform-wide inheritsModelFrom chain only; a scoped override of the parent, or a parent edited later, fails with HARNESS_UNSUPPORTED_MODEL when a run resolves it. A new override starts on the platform-wide row’s runtime, but a later change to that row’s runtime does not reach existing overrides.
limits.title: Some runtimes pin at first use, not at run start

limits.body: Scheduled regression runs pass no runtime override, and a runtime breakdown sees only offline harness rows.
limits.detail: The scheduled eval prepares its run from a dataset slug and two refs only, so the nightly gate uses each agent’s resolved runtime. Online result rows carry no runtime, the runtime column holds the candidate’s runtime only, and a template-filtered trend excludes harness rows, so a runtime split there has no runtime values.
limits.title: Runtime comparisons cover manual eval runs and harness rows only

limits.body: The binary is hashed by sha256sum inside the workspace, which the agent can modify.
limits.detail: The check catches a replaced or damaged copy between turns, but it relies on the container’s sha256sum, which the agent can write. It runs before each turn, not during one, and needs sha256sum in the image.
limits.title: The harness binary check trusts the container’s sha256sum

limits.body: A harness is admitted only if the worker answers each of its tool calls before the call runs.
limits.detail: A harness must ask the worker before every tool call over a channel the worker owns, wait for the answer, not run a refused call, and offer no repository or container file that can grant a call without that answer. The registry refuses any harness that does not declare this, with HARNESS_POLICY_UNENFORCEABLE. A harness supplies only provisioning, a mapping of its tools onto the canonical vocabulary, usage normalisation and the turn protocol; binary verification, process cleanup, cancellation, the decision deadline and trace bounding are shared.
limits.title: Claude Code is the only harness the worker admits

limits.body: Memory gate refusals and recall drops are security events, but a drop is reported at most hourly per row and per process, and the gate matches patterns, not intent.
limits.detail: Lesson, consolidation and channel writes refused for a match are MEMORY_WRITE_REFUSED events and dropped recalled items MEMORY_RECALL_DROPPED, carrying ids and pattern names, never the text. A drop is reported once per memory id per hour per worker process, written in the background so recall does not wait; a drop of another team’s channel row records only a count. An event raised outside an activity, or whose trace write fails, is only logged, and a write refused because an INJECTION pattern overran or is quarantined is traced as an outage (memory.write_scan_unavailable), not a refusal. A consolidation whose scan failed, did not complete or could not load is traced the same way (memory.consolidation_scan_unavailable). These outage events are ordinary activity events in the run’s trace; the security-events view lists and counts only matches and recall drops, so a pattern outage that is stopping memory writes appears in no security count. A write whose pattern set could not load is thrown (commitToMemory) or logged, not traced. On such a load failure recall returns nothing. The fence labels memory as reference data; it does not stop a reworded instruction that no INJECTION pattern matches.
limits.title: Memory refusals are pattern-based, drop reports are throttled, and a scan outage is not a security event

limits.body: The saver passes a launch decision when an enabled automation is saved or enabled; when it fires, nothing re-checks the saver.
limits.detail: A fire checks the repository, the kill switch, the organization’s monthly budget and the limits, not the saver’s continued access or role. The run carries no launchedById and uses the platform credential. The label source is the exception in attribution only: the person who added the label must be an active platform user whose linked GitHub account matches, a member of the repository, and pass the launch decision at that moment; that user is recorded as requestedById and the run still acts as the platform. The check exists because an issue form adds labels on behalf of whoever opens the issue, so the label alone says nothing about who asked.
limits.title: An automation runs as the platform, not as the person who saved it

limits.body: Nothing polls the host for a failure or a label the platform was not told about.
limits.detail: The engine retries a start three times (after one and two seconds) and then answers 503, so a host that redelivers recovers; one that does not leaves a FAILED_TO_START decision for a manager to retry. Turning a kill switch off stops later decisions; it does not stop runs already started.
limits.title: Automation decisions rest on the webhook; a missed delivery is not recovered

limits.body: The template has no human node and no review network; the fix is reviewed only as part of the pull request it lands on.
limits.detail: Before the push a fix must pass the implementer’s path guard (workflow and action files, symlinks and submodules refused), the implementer’s security gate, the push step’s own checks and its own workflow-path check on the pushed range. Lint, typecheck and tests run too, but their failures are warnings and do not stop delivery. Verification labels the fix but does not gate it. The push step re-checks workflow paths only, not symlinks; that refusal lives in the implementer’s guard. Draft fixes are revised up to maxCiFixAttempts, while a pushed fix gets at most one follow-up.
limits.title: A pushed CI fix has no approval step

limits.body: A log that evades the INJECTION patterns reaches the implementer fenced as data, with the path guard behind it.
limits.detail: Redaction covers common token shapes only. The screen uses INJECTION patterns only, and the template-injection pattern is excluded because ordinary build output matches it. With more than ten failed jobs, the implementer’s per-job excerpt (4,000 characters) is longer than the share of the screened tail each job got, so part of it was never screened. A scan that cannot complete counts as not clean, so such a log is diagnosed but never fixed from.
limits.title: CI log screening is pattern-based

limits.body: Only the whole run: of a failed step without Actions expressions is run, and nothing is installed first.
limits.detail: Setup-dependent failures read as unverified or still failing; a command that passes before the fix reads as not reproduced. The workflow file is read from the failing branch’s tip in the workspace, not from the failing commit.
limits.title: Verification runs only a whole failed step’s command

limits.body: A changed built-in input schema reaches an existing deployment only if its stored schema equals one recorded in the previous-schemas map.
limits.detail: Sync moves a built-in template’s input schema only while the template is active on its latest built-in version, runs no A/B experiment, and stores a schema an earlier release shipped; anything else is treated as an admin edit and kept. A built-in schema change not added to that map reaches fresh databases only. ci-triage-and-fix has no entry in the map.
limits.title: Built-in input schemas move forward only from a schema a release shipped

limits.body: STARTED rows and rows naming something the platform produced are kept for good.
limits.detail: Event-automation rows that started a run grow at most by each automation’s daily cap; every schedule fire or template webhook call that started a run adds one permanent row, with no cap. The sweep deletes the rest in batches of 2,000, up to 50 batches a run, and continues the next day; it covers every source, so old schedule and webhook refusals go with the event suppressions.
limits.title: Started decisions are never pruned

limits.body: The coverage model never decrypts a key or calls a provider, and the dashboard’s delete sends force.
limits.detail: A revoked or wrong key reads as covered. The worker’s boot gate resolves each GLOBAL agent for real and checks the embedding model’s rows only, so the two implementations of one rule can disagree on an edge (the coverage check also requires an apiBase on any non-built-in provider’s credential, agent or embedding, which the boot gate does not check). A channel or workflow-template agent counts any credential for its provider. The delete guard protects API callers: the dashboard’s delete confirmation lists what the delete would strand and then sends force=true, and a forced delete by a team admin audits only the dependents that admin may see. The per-provider flag on the readiness route is derived from the same rows, so it inherits that blindness and also follows the embedding rule above: an embedding fault that is not a missing credential or an unpinned apiBase never marks a provider, so an agent on that provider shows no badge for it.
limits.title: Coverage checks rows, not keys, and the dashboard always forces

limits.body: A model or embedding call to a host that resolves to a private address fails unless the host is listed, and so does a provider that answers with a redirect.
limits.detail: A host that resolved publicly when a credential was saved and privately later is caught now, but an admin must list a legitimate internal host. A listed name is trusted to mean the server intended: any private-range address it resolves to is reachable, and only loopback, link-local and metadata addresses stay refused. The list is global to every credential, and under an environment proxy the check is not pinned.
limits.title: Guarded model calls fail closed for in-cluster and redirecting providers

limits.body: Custom providers get the response schema as prompt text, which a model can ignore.
limits.detail: Compatible embedding endpoints without truncation support only work at a native 1536 width. Pricing keys off the canonical provider/model spec text, so a model reached through a proxy is priced by the spec, not by what the proxy actually serves.
limits.title: Provider differences are bridged, not erased

limits.body: When the poll on the pushed commit times out or loses access, the run ends SUCCESS “Fix pushed” with no CI verdict.
limits.detail: The watch step continues on error, so a poll deadline or a failed fetch takes the same path as a pass: the work branch is removed and the run ends as pushed. The commit’s later failure is still recognised as the platform’s own output and not acted on again, so nobody is told it failed unless someone reads the pull request’s checks.
limits.title: A pushed fix’s CI watch that cannot finish still ends the run as pushed

limits.body: The model guard is passed as fetch to each client the worker builds; a client built another way would not have it.
limits.detail: The worker re-exports the raw provider constructors, and the bare-fetch invariant is a text tripwire that does not see an SDK constructor called without a fetch option. A new client added outside the two model-building modules would call its host unchecked until someone passes the guard to it.
limits.title: Nothing enforces the guard on a new provider client

limits.body: Glossary definitions, node help and inline help are static prose; tests check that their doc links resolve and that examples parse, not that the sentences are true.
limits.detail: The glossary says its definitions are written to agree with the concepts doc, and the link table says a test checks each entry against the docs files and headings. Neither derives a definition from the code, so a behaviour change can leave a tip stale while every link still resolves. Node help, the tour steps and the run verdict sentences are hand-written constants too; tests parse each node example with the real schema, assert a few of the node gotchas and check that every tour anchor exists in the sidebar, but most sentences are not checked against behaviour. The reader and its search show the docs shipped with the web app, so a running deployment can show docs older than its gateway, and both cover only the top-level docs, so a link to or a search for anything else would not resolve. Tips, the checklist, the tour, node help and the verdict are shown in the dashboard only; the CLI and API have no equivalent.
limits.title: Help text is hand-written and only its links and examples are checked
